Measuring aid and remittances in small island developing states

From the national figure to the household

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Malta
Today, block one

How each kind of money is counted, and where the figures are published

We define aid and remittances, look at what each official figure includes and leaves out, and open every data source on the screen for Tonga. We then ask who decides how each kind of money is used, and how that decision can be seen from the household.

Tomorrow, block two

Your island, mapped

In the first half hour you find three figures for your own country with me in the room. Your group then maps how aid and remittances reach households on your island and presents the map, which is the basis of your classwork and your assignment.

Good afternoon. My name is Roxane de Waegh, and I am a Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral fellow here at the Islands and Small States Institute. My project, FAR-SIDS, studies foreign aid and remittances in small island developing states, and these two sessions draw on that work.

Today and tomorrow form one piece of work: today I explain how aid and remittances are defined and counted, and I open, on the screen, the websites where the figures for your own country are published. Tomorrow you work in country groups, you find those figures yourselves in the first half hour, and you then map how the two kinds of money reach households on your island. That map is the material for your classwork and for your assignment, so everything we cover today is something you will use tomorrow. This module uses the terms that economists and ministries use, because you will meet them in every report written about your country. Whenever I use one of those terms for the first time, I will explain it in plain words, and the explanation stays on the screen beside the term.

The question for this week

Two kinds of money arrive on an island. What does each one do for the people in the house?

The answer has four parts: what the money paid for, who decided, who it reached and who it missed, and what the household gave up to get it.

Here is the question for this week, and it is the one sentence I would like you to keep when you have forgotten the rest. Two kinds of money arrive on an island from outside: aid, which a foreign government sends to your government, and remittances, which a relative abroad sends to a family. What does each one do for the people in the house?

I ask it that way because the question a ministry usually asks is a different one: how much arrived. That figure is published every year for every island, and we spend part one on where to find it. It tells you how much money crossed the border, and then it stops. Every decision that uses it assumes that more money arriving means that households are better off, and nobody has checked that on these islands.

Why does the answer matter? Because it changes what a government does with the money it has. After a cyclone, a ministry that knows which households already receive money from relatives can send its own recovery money first to the households that do not. A government that signs a seasonal work agreement can negotiate the number of places and the length of the season knowing what the families at home lose while the worker is away. A programme that pays cash to households can be sized knowing whether the relative abroad sends less once the programme pays. And a statistics office can start measuring whether households are better off, instead of whether more money arrived. For the households themselves it means that what they give up, which today is counted nowhere, becomes something a government can see and answer for.

One more reason to ask it here, with you. No survey anywhere asks a household about aid and remittances in the same house, so the databases hold no answer to this question yet. You come from these islands, and you know things about how money moves inside a family that no database holds. That is why tomorrow you draw your own island, and why my own project, FAR-SIDS, asks this question in Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros with a household survey, interviews and the national figures together. This week does the same thing at the size of one classroom. We start with the figures, because you have to know what a figure counts before you can say what it leaves out.

The question for this week · the two kinds of money

Aid and remittances: the two kinds of money

Aid, which the reports call official development assistanceMoney that a foreign government, or an official body such as the World Bank, gives to your government or lends to it on cheaper terms than a bank would. It is public money that passes between governments. When France pays for a new maternity ward in Moroni, that is aid.
A remittanceMoney that a relative working abroad sends home to the family. It is private money that passes between people. When your cousin in Marseille sends 200 euros for school fees, that is a remittance.

The two kinds of money, once, in plain terms. Aid, which every report you will read calls official development assistance, is money that a foreign government or an official body such as the World Bank gives to your government, or lends to it on cheaper terms than a bank would, so it is public money passing between governments. A remittance is money that a relative working abroad sends home, so it is private money passing between people. When your cousin in Marseille sends 200 euros for school fees, that is a remittance, and when France pays for a new maternity ward in Moroni, that is aid.

Both are counted every year, and in part one we look at how each is counted and where the figures are published, opening the real websites for Tonga. In part two we ask why a dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance are used differently once they arrive, and in part three we move from the national figure to the household and to what a ministry could do with that knowledge.

Part one

Counting aid and remittances

Every published figure follows counting rules. Before you use a figure, you need to know what those rules include, what they leave out, and where the figure for your own country is published.

How each is counted

The four conditions a payment meets to count as aid, and the two kinds of money inside the remittance line.

What each figure leaves out

Donors that report to nobody, and the money and goods that never pass through a bank.

Where your own figures are published

Eight sources, each opened on the screen for Tonga as we come to it.

A figureA number that an organisation publishes, for example "Tonga’s remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024" (World Bank, n.d.). Every figure was built by somebody who counted something according to rules.
The national accountsThe government's yearly record of the whole economy: what the country produced, earned and spent, and what came in from other countries and went out to them. The aid and remittance figures are taken from these accounts.
Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Personal remittances, received (% of GDP) (BX.TRF.PWKR.DT.GD.ZS) [Data set]. World Development Indicators. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.DT.GD.ZS?locations=TO

A statement such as "Tonga’s remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024" is read as a plain fact about a country, when it is the result of a count, and the rules of that count decide what is included and what is left out. By the end of this part you will be able to find the aid and remittance figures for your own island and explain what each of them measures and what it does not. We start with the scale of the two flows, then define each of them, and open each website where your own figures are published as we come to it.

Two words for this part. A figure is a published number, and every figure was built by somebody who counted something according to rules. The national accounts are the government's yearly record of the whole economy, of what the country produced and earned and of what came in from abroad and went out, and the aid and remittance figures quoted in reports are taken from those accounts. So when you read that Tonga’s remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024, somebody counted, under rules, and part one is about those rules.

Part one · The scale of the two flows

Pacific islands receive more of aid and remittances than any other developing group

Every bar is a World Bank country group in 2021, the latest year for which the World Bank publishes the aid share of the groups. Remittances are divided by GDP and aid by GNI because that is how the World Bank publishes each one (World Bank, n.d.-a; World Bank, n.d.-b).

GDP, gross domestic productThe value of everything a country produces inside its borders in a year, the usual measure of the size of an economy. Remittances are earned abroad, so they are not part of it.
GNI, gross national incomeGDP plus what the country's residents earn abroad, minus what foreigners earn inside it. A seasonal worker abroad for seven months is still a resident, so her wages are in GNI. A daughter settled in Auckland is not, so what she sends is in neither.
A share of GDP or GNIThe money that arrived, divided by the size of the economy. At 12.7% of GDP, for every 100 dollars the Pacific island economies produced in 2021, 12 dollars and 70 cents arrived from relatives abroad on top.
The four groupsPacific island states and Caribbean island states are the World Bank's groups of small island states in each region. Least developed countries is the United Nations list of the poorest countries. Low and middle income countries is every developing country together.
Sources

Ratha, D., Chandra, V., Kim, E. J., Jammeh, K., Riordan, E., & Vezmar, M. (2021). Recovery: COVID-19 crisis through a migration lens (Migration and Development Brief No. 35). World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099738408132414027/pdf/IDU110e1541c1704b14821196441e301ab86ff0b.pdf

World Bank. (2020). COVID-19 crisis through a migration lens (Migration and Development Brief No. 32). https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/33634

World Bank. (n.d.-a). Personal remittances, received (% of GDP) [Data set]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.DT.GD.ZS

World Bank. (n.d.-b). Net ODA received (% of GNI) [Data set]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.GN.ZS

World Bank. (n.d.-c). GNI (current US$) [Data set, metadata]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GNP.MKTP.CD

GDP, gross domestic product, is the value of everything a country produces inside its own borders in a year, and it is the usual measure of how large an economy is. Remittances are not part of it. That money is earned abroad, by a daughter in Auckland or a son in Sydney, and it arrives on top of what Tonga itself produced. So when the World Bank says that remittances were 12.7% of GDP across the Pacific island states in 2021, it means that for every 100 dollars those economies produced in the year, another 12 dollars and 70 cents came in from relatives working abroad. The figure is a division: money arriving from abroad on top, production at home underneath. Because the top and the bottom are two different things, the figure is not a slice of a whole. Tonga's remittances were 41.5% of its GDP in 2021 (World Bank, n.d.-a), and that does not mean that 41.5% of what Tonga produced was remittances. It means that for every 100 pa'anga Tonga produced, another 41 and a half arrived from abroad on top.

Here is a question before we go on. If the transfer itself is not part of GDP, does the money ever appear in GDP at all? Think about the 12 dollars and 70 cents. The transfer does not enter GDP, because nothing was produced in Tonga to earn it. What the family does with it can. A mother in Ha'apai spends it on fish from a fisherman in her village, on her son's school fees and on a sheet of roofing iron from a hardware store in Nuku'alofa. The fisherman's catch, the school's teaching and the store's sale are all production inside Tonga, so they are counted in Tonga's GDP. The money came in once from outside and was then earned again inside the country. Now a second question: is it good when the number underneath the division, production at home, goes up? If it goes up because the money was spent on things made at home, then yes, that is the effect economists hope remittances will have, and notice what it does to the figure on the screen. The same amount of money arrives, production at home is larger, so the share falls. A falling share can mean less money arriving, or it can mean a growing economy, and only the amount in dollars tells you which. So across years, read the amount in dollars as well as the share.

And what if the money is spent on things made somewhere else? The same mother buys a phone made in China from a shop in Nuku'alofa, rice grown in Thailand and petrol refined in Singapore. That production happened in those countries and is counted in their GDP. The shop in Tonga keeps its margin, and most of the money leaves Tonga again to pay the importer. So the share on the screen tells you how much money arrived, measured against the size of the economy. It does not tell you whether the money stayed. That depends on what it was spent on and on who decided, and that is where Part two of today goes.

Now read the two charts. Every bar is a World Bank country group in 2021, the latest year for which the World Bank publishes the aid share for the groups, and both charts come from the two pages you will open yourself in the next demonstrations (World Bank, n.d.-a; World Bank, n.d.-b). Aid is divided by gross national income, GNI, because that is how the World Bank publishes it. GNI starts from GDP, adds what the country's residents earn abroad and subtracts what foreigners earn inside the country (World Bank, n.d.-c). The word that matters is resident. A Tongan who goes to New Zealand for seven months of seasonal work is still counted as living in Tonga, so her wages are part of Tonga's GNI. Her sister who settled in Auckland ten years ago is counted as living in New Zealand, and the money she sends home is a transfer between two countries, so it sits outside both GDP and GNI. For most islands the two totals are close, and the rule at the end of this part asks you to say which one a figure uses. Now the bars. The Pacific island states received 12.7% of GDP in remittances and 16.8% of GNI in aid, far above the least developed countries, the poorest group in the world, at 4.5% and 4.7%, and far above the average for all low and middle income countries at 1.5% and 0.6%. The Caribbean island states sit below the least developed countries on both counts, at 2.5% and 1.2%. So small island states are not one group, and a figure for the Pacific does not describe the Caribbean. Every bar is also an average across very different countries. Our three islands in the same year: Tonga 41.5% of GDP in remittances and 20.7% of GNI in aid, the Comoros 22.2% and 12.0%, Jamaica 23.2% and 0.4% (World Bank, n.d.-a; World Bank, n.d.-b). Jamaica's remittance figure is above the Comoros and its aid figure is close to nothing. If you worked in Jamaica's planning ministry, which of the two flows would you spend your time on?

A figure published under a large name still has to be checked. In April 2020 the World Bank forecast that remittances to low and middle income countries would fall by 19.7% during the pandemic (World Bank, 2020). They fell by 1.7%, and in 2021 they rose by 7.3% (Ratha et al., 2021). Families abroad sent more money, not less, when their relatives at home lost work. Does anyone here know the remittance figure for their own country? Most people do not, and by the middle of this part you will be able to find it in under a minute.

Part one · What counts as aid

A payment counts as aid only if it meets four conditions

  1. It comes from a government or an official agency, and not from a charity, a company or a private person.
  2. It goes to a country on the OECD list of aid recipients, which includes every small island developing state except those classed as high income.
  3. Its main purpose is the development and welfare of that country, so military spending and loans that promote the donor's exports do not count.
  4. It is a grant, or a loan on cheaper terms than a bank would give. A grant is money the country keeps and never repays. A loan is repaid, and it is aid only when the interest is lower and the time to repay longer than a bank would offer. A loan at the market interest rate is not aid, even when a government makes it.
OECDThe Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, an organisation of mostly high income countries based in Paris. Its Development Assistance Committee, the DAC, writes the rules for what counts as aid.
Who counts itEach donor government reports its own spending to the OECD against these rules, so every aid figure for your country is built from what the donors reported.
ConcessionalThe term for a loan on cheaper terms than the market offers, with a lower interest rate and a longer time to repay than a bank would give.
The OECD definition
Sources

OECD. (n.d.). Official development assistance (ODA): Definition and coverage. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/oda-eligibility-and-conditions/official-development-assistance--definition-and-coverage.html

OECD. (2026). Converged statistical reporting directives for the Creditor Reporting System (CRS) and the Annual DAC Questionnaire (DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL). https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL/en/pdf

The scale slide gave you the size of the two flows. Before we open the page where the aid figure is published, we need to know what that figure counts, because the rules decide what is in it. The OECD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is an organisation of mostly high income countries based in Paris, and its Development Assistance Committee, a committee of about thirty donor governments known as the DAC, writes the rules for what counts as aid. Under those rules, a payment is official development assistance only if it meets four conditions.

The payment must come from a government or an official agency rather than from a charity or a company. It must go to a country on the OECD list of aid recipients, and every small island developing state except those classed as high income is on that list. Its main purpose must be the development and welfare of that country, which excludes military spending and loans that promote the donor's exports. Finally, it must be a grant or a cheap loan. A grant is money the country keeps and never repays. A loan is repaid, and it counts as aid only when the interest is lower and the repayment period longer than a bank would offer, which the rules call concessional, so a loan at the market interest rate is not aid even when a government makes it.

The donors also do the counting, since each donor government reports its own spending to the OECD against these rules, so the figure is defined by the governments that send the money, for their own accounting. The next demonstration opens the page where the World Bank publishes the figure built from those reports, and the one after it opens the table where the donors report. Before that, here is a question for you: is a Chinese government loan to Tonga at a commercial interest rate aid? It is not, because it fails the fourth condition, and there is a second reason, which we come to shortly: China does not report to the OECD.

Three islands, three positions. Tonga receives a fifth of its national income in aid, the Comoros a ninth, and Jamaica almost none. Tonga's own figure was two and a half times higher the year before.

What this source cannot tell you. Who paid it. This page gives one total for all donors together, and the next demonstration breaks that total into the donors that paid it.

Why this matters

Dividing by national income is what makes an island of 100,000 people comparable with a country of three million. The figure says how much aid arrived and nothing about why. One island can change in a year: Tonga's share was 50.7% in 2022, when relief aid followed the eruption of the Hunga Tonga volcano in January of that year, and 20.3% in 2023. Between islands, a gap can come from the donors' own rules, which give less as a country's income rises, from where donors choose to concentrate, as Australia and New Zealand do in the Pacific, or from a disaster in that year. The figure alone cannot say which, so write the year beside every figure you take from this page. The next demonstration shows who paid it.

You now know the four conditions a payment meets to count as aid. This is the page where the figure built from the donors' reports is published, and the aid chart on the scale slide came from it, so this is the first place to go for any island. I am opening the link on this slide, which lands on the World Bank page for Tonga, and I would like you to open it on your own laptop as we go. The page gives one number for each country for each year: all the aid the country received that year, after subtracting what it repaid on earlier aid loans, divided by gross national income, GNI, which we defined on the scale slide as GDP plus what residents earn abroad minus what foreigners earn inside the country. The World Bank uses GNI for aid because the donors' rules on which countries may receive aid are written in terms of GNI per person, and dividing by it is what lets a small island be compared with a large country.

Follow the four clicks on the slide with me. When you type in the search box, a list drops down as you type, and the line you want reads exactly Net ODA received (% of GNI). One line away from it sits Net ODA provided, which is what donor countries give away, and if you click that one by mistake you get an empty map, because Tonga gives no aid. The page opens for the whole world, so scroll down to the list called All Countries and Economies and click your country, and the chart redraws for it. I am doing that now for Tonga, and now for Jamaica, so you can see the whole page change. That is how you switch country.

Now read the grey text under the title with me. It says the numbers come from the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD, and that World Bank estimates of national income are used for the bottom of the division. So this page and the OECD table in the next demonstration are not two organisations counting separately. They are the same donor returns, with the World Bank dividing them by its own estimate of the size of the economy. When the two disagree it is because one is gross and the other is net, or because one was revised later, and not because two counts of the same money came out differently.

Look at the gap between the three islands on the slide: Tonga at 20.3, the Comoros at 11.3 and Jamaica at 0.4 in 2023. Why might an island in the Caribbean receive so little aid, measured against its economy, compared with an island in the Pacific? Think about that for a moment before I say anything. Several answers are possible, and this figure cannot choose between them. Jamaica's economy is many times larger than Tonga's, so the same number of dollars is a much smaller share. The donors' rules give less aid as a country's income per person rises. Donors concentrate where they have history and interests, and Australia and New Zealand concentrate on the Pacific in the way France concentrates on the Comoros. And a disaster in that year raises the figure: Tonga's share was 50.7% in 2022, when relief followed the eruption of the Hunga Tonga volcano in January, and 20.3% in 2023. So when you write a figure like this into your map, write the year beside it and ask what happened in that year. What this page cannot tell you is who paid, and that is the next demonstration.

If this page has moved by the time you look for it, search for the exact phrase Net ODA received % of GNI World Bank, and the first result is this page. If your island is not one of our three, it is on this same page, because every country in the world is in the list under the chart.

The slide on what counts as aid said that the donors do the counting. This is the table where they report it, and the link on this slide lands on the finished table for Tonga. I am going to clear the filters and build it again from the beginning, so you can see where each number comes from, and you can build it with me.

First, what this database is. It holds one row for every project that a reporting donor funded, anywhere in the world, going back decades. The filters on the left decide which rows you see, and three of them decide everything: who received the money, who gave it, and in which year.

The donor step is the one that goes wrong. The database opens with the donors collapsed into one line called DAC countries, which gives one number and hides the list. Deselect All followed by Select All is what opens the list out. The site only offers donors that actually paid this country, so Select All is safe here and will not give you the whole world.

Look at the shape of the table, because it is a tree rather than a flat list. Official donors is everything. Underneath it sit DAC countries, then Non-DAC countries, then Multilateral organisations, and under each of those the individual donors. Australia is already inside DAC countries, and the International Development Association is already inside Multilateral organisations, so if you add the individual rows to the group rows you count the same money twice.

Now the words at the top of the table, which you should write down: gross disbursements, constant 2024 prices. Gross means before subtracting anything the country repaid, so this figure is larger than the World Bank net figure in the previous demonstration for the same country and the same year. Constant prices means the amounts have been adjusted so that years can be compared. Disbursements means money actually paid, as against commitments, which is money promised and may arrive years later or not at all.

When you click Download, you get a file with one row for every line of this table and a lot of empty columns. Ignore the empty ones. The three things you need are the donor name, the year and the amount, and the amount is in millions of US dollars, so 68.068 on the Australia row is 68 million dollars.

Now, in your group, find the three largest donors to your own island. Is any of them a country you would not have guessed?

Part one · What the aid figure leaves out

The OECD report

The three rows are the 2024 disbursements you pulled in the last demonstration, the money actually paid that year. The same database also holds each commitment, the amount promised when the agreement was signed, and the two can be years apart (OECD, 2026).

Promised money and paid money

Commitments and disbursements

A commitment is the amount promised when an agreement is signed, and a disbursement is the amount actually paid. Payment can arrive years later, or not at all, so ask for disbursements.

Who received it

The country and the sector

A row names the donor, the receiving country, the sector, such as health, roads or education, and the amount. Two further boxes, for the agency the money passed through and for the town or region, are optional and often empty. No row names a village, a household or a person.

A question for you

Australia's row says 68.1 million dollars paid to Tonga in 2024. From that row alone, what can you say about who in Tonga received it, and what can you not say?

Sources

OECD. (2026). Converged statistical reporting directives for the Creditor Reporting System (CRS) and the Annual DAC Questionnaire (DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL). https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC(2026)14/FINAL/en/pdf

The OECD database is the most careful record of aid that exists, and it still leaves out three things that matter for small islands. Look at the table you have just built. The three rows on the screen are the 2024 disbursements you pulled: Australia 68.1 million US dollars, New Zealand 30.6 million and the World Bank's International Development Association 29.6 million. Every row names the donor, the country that received the money, the sector, such as health, roads or education, and the amount. It also has a box for the agency the money passed through, which can be the recipient government or one of its ministries, and the reporting rules give donors one optional box of 100 characters, called the geographical target area, for the town or region a project is meant to benefit (OECD, 2026). Both boxes are optional and donors rarely fill them. No row names a village, a household or a person. So the record shows which country a programme reached and not who inside the country it reached, which makes it hard to say afterwards how well a programme worked, and it is one reason so few studies have looked at aid and remittances together at the household level. That is the first gap. Take the question on the slide: from Australia's row you can say that 68.1 million dollars was paid to Tonga in 2024 and which sectors it went to, and you cannot say which island, which village or which household any of it reached. Tomorrow you fill that gap for one household by asking, which no database can do for you.

The second gap is between promised money and paid money. The database separates commitments from disbursements, where a commitment is the amount promised on the day an agreement is signed and a disbursement is the amount actually paid out. The two can be years apart, and a commitment can be cancelled, so when you take a figure from the database, ask for disbursements, as the table you built did.

The third gap is the dashed row at the bottom of the screen. Every figure in this database is built from what donors choose to report, and reporting is voluntary. A government that does not report has no row, and its money is missing from every figure built on this database, including the World Bank aid share we opened first. The largest such lender to Tonga is China, and the next demonstration shows where its money is counted.

Who else paid your island, and how would you know?

Tonga
419.4 m, 180 projects
Jamaica

In the OECD table, the Comoros receives 17.685 million from non-DAC governments in 2024, of which Saudi Arabia 11.281 and the United Arab Emirates 6.188.

Do not add these to the OECD figure. The OECD figure is money paid in one year at 2024 prices. AidData is money promised since 2000 at 2023 prices. Two different questions, two different answers.

What Tonga still owes. At the end of June 2024 Tonga's external debt was 157 million US dollars, and 47% of it, about 74 million, was owed to the Export Import Bank of China, the single largest creditor (World Bank & IMF, 2025). That is a debt still outstanding, not money paid in a year.

What this source cannot tell you. How much of the promised money has actually been paid out, and which household any of it reached. Every source on this slide counts money at the level of the country or the project.

Why this matters

None of China’s 419 million dollars to Tonga appears in the OECD table or in the World Bank aid share, so a student who uses only those two sources leaves out the largest single lender to the country. In the downloaded file, 142 of Tonga’s 180 Chinese projects are grants and only 5 are loans, but the two largest loans, 96 million dollars for the Nuku’alofa business district in 2007 and 55 million for roads in 2010, are worth more than all 142 grants together. The list reads like a list of gifts, and most of the money is debt.

Sources

AidData. (n.d.). Global Chinese Development Finance Dashboard. William & Mary. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://china.aiddata.org/

OECD. (n.d.). CRS: Creditor Reporting System (flows) [Data set]. OECD Data Explorer. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://data-explorer.oecd.org/

World Bank & International Monetary Fund. (2025). Tonga: Joint World Bank and IMF debt sustainability analysis. World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099012326152552028/pdf/BOSIB-caf655fa-adfc-4b75-8ed3-a9712975fdb8.pdf

This slide exists because the OECD figures are built from what donors report, and reporting is voluntary. A government that does not report has no row, and its money is missing from every figure built on that database, including the World Bank aid share in the aid share demonstration. China is the largest such donor, and it does not report.

Start with the part of the OECD table that most people scroll past, the branch called Non-DAC countries. These governments report even though they are not members of the committee. Open the table for the Comoros and you find Saudi Arabia at 11.3 million and the United Arab Emirates at 6.2 million sitting there, so those governments are not missing, they are under a heading nobody opens.

For China we need a different site. Open china.aiddata.org with me. Click Filters & Search, then Geographic Filters, then the tab Countries; type Tonga, tick it, and click Update Filters. Two figures appear at the top: 180 projects, and 419 million US dollars committed. Now I am doing the same for Jamaica: 129 projects and 2.4 billion dollars. Two and a half billion dollars of Chinese commitments to Jamaica appear nowhere in the aid figures you would otherwise find for Jamaica. That is the point of this slide.

Be careful with the word commitment. AidData counts commitments and the OECD table counted disbursements. A commitment is money promised in an agreement; a disbursement is money paid. Tonga’s 419 million is what China promised over twenty five years, not what arrived last year, and putting it beside the OECD’s 150.9 million for 2024 compares two different things. If you use both figures, label both.

Now click Download Data and open the file named CLG_Global1.0_Filtered. It has one row per Chinese project in Tonga since 2000, 180 rows, and far more columns than anyone needs. Look only at three: Title, Flow_Type and Amount_Constant_USD_2023. Click the heading of the Flow_Type column and sort it A to Z, so that the loans sit together: 142 of the 180 rows say Grant and only 5 say Loan. So is China generous to Tonga? Most people say yes at this point. Now sort by Amount_Constant_USD_2023, largest first, and read the top two rows: a 96 million dollar loan from China Eximbank in 2007 for the Nuku’alofa central business district, and a 55 million dollar loan in 2010 for roads. Those two loans are worth more than all 142 grants together. The grants are school buildings, sports fields, scholarships and disaster supplies, real things, and almost all of them small; the money is in the loans, and loans are repaid. Tonga’s whole economy is about 650 million dollars a year.

Where does the figure of 47% on the slide come from, and why is it a different kind of number from everything else on this slide? The World Bank and the IMF publish a debt sustainability analysis for Tonga, a report on whether the country can keep paying what it owes, and the edition published in November 2025 lists Tonga's external debt by lender at the end of June 2024: 157 million US dollars in total, of which 47% was owed to the Export Import Bank of China, the largest single creditor, ahead of the World Bank's International Development Association at 26% (World Bank & IMF, 2025). External debt is money a country owes to lenders in other countries. So AidData's 419 million is what China promised since 2000, the OECD table shows what reporting donors paid in one year, and the 47% is what is still owed today, largely from the two loans of 2007 and 2010. The same report notes that Tonga's repayments to that bank peaked in the 2024 financial year at 3% of GDP. Three sources answer three different questions, and only the last one is money Tonga still has to pay.

Here is the question to sit with. A government that looks at this list sees 142 gifts and 5 loans. The same government, ten years later, is repaying the loans out of a budget that also has to pay for schools and clinics. Who in the country is carrying those two loans today, and did the households that received the gifts have any say in the loans that came with them? There is no single right answer, and you will meet the repayment figure again on the grants and loans slide this afternoon.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search AidData China global development finance dashboard. If your island is not one of our three, the pair of sources is the same everywhere: the Non-DAC branch of the OECD table for governments that report, and AidData for China. If your island has a large lender that appears in neither, say so in your map and name where you looked, because that absence is itself a finding.

If your island is in the Pacific, one more site does in one page what the last two demonstrations did in two. I am opening pacificaidmap.lowyinstitute.org and clicking Explore the map. Read the four numbers at the top with me: 2.5 billion US dollars spent, 2.9 billion committed, 3,135 projects, and 86% for status. Spent means money actually paid out; committed means money promised; the gap between them is money that has been announced and has not yet arrived. Status is the share of projects whose progress Lowy has been able to trace. The Lowy Institute does not wait for donors to report. The map covers fourteen Pacific countries and nothing else. If your island is in the Caribbean or the Indian Ocean, the OECD table and AidData remain your two sources for who paid.

Part one · What counts as a remittance

How to measure remittances

What the remittance line adds together
Part one · Personal transfers

Money sent by someone who has lived abroad for a year or more.

For example, a cousin in Auckland for ten years.
+
Part two · Compensation of employees

The pay of someone working abroad on a contract of less than a year.

For example, a seasonal worker picking fruit.

Together, the two parts make up the remittance line of the balance of payments.

The companies whose reports build the figure
The balance of paymentsThe record that every central bank keeps of the money that crosses the border in a year, in both directions: exports, imports, loans, aid and remittances. GDP counts what is produced inside the country; the balance of payments counts what moves in and out of it. Remittances are one line of this record, made of the two parts above.
The one year ruleA person abroad for a year or more counts as living in the other country, so what they send home is a transfer. A person abroad for less than a year still counts as living at home, so their whole pay is counted as income, whether or not they send it home.
How the figure is builtBanks and money transfer companies report to the central bank the money they received from abroad and handed over here, and the central bank adds those reports together. No household is asked what it received.
TongaThe National Reserve Bank of Tonga publishes remittances in four categories, and the pay of Tongans working abroad, which is where the seasonal workers appear, is one of them.
Sources

Maeda, H., Edwards, R., & Suryadarma, D. (2024, February 14). Customer choices are keeping Pacific remittance costs high. Devpolicy Blog. https://devpolicy.org/customer-choices-are-keeping-pacific-remittance-costs-high-20240214/

Bank of Jamaica. (n.d.). List of remittance companies. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://boj.org.jm/core-functions/financial-system/list-of-remittance-companies/

da Cruz, V., Fengler, W., & Schwartzman, A. (2004). Remittances to Comoros: Volume, trends, impact and implications (Africa Region Working Paper Series No. 75). World Bank. https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/957391468772177750/pdf/312750PAPER0Comoros0AFR0wp75.pdf

International Monetary Fund. (n.d.). Annex 4: Remittances [Draft annex to the balance of payments and international investment position manual, 7th ed.]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/data/statistics/bmp7/draft-chapters/bpm7-annex-4-v7-remittances.pdf

National Reserve Bank of Tonga. (n.d.). Economic reviews: monthly economic update and remittances. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.reservebank.to/

Remittances are counted in a different way, through the balance of payments that every central bank keeps, which is the record of all the money that came into the country and went out of it during a year, including exports, imports, loans, aid and remittances. GDP, which we met on the scale slide, counts what is produced inside the country. The balance of payments counts what crosses the border, so remittances appear in the second and never in the first. Remittances are one line of that record, and the line adds two parts together. The first is personal transfers, which is the money sent home by someone who has lived abroad for a year or more, such as a cousin who has been in Auckland for ten years. The second is what accountants call compensation of employees, which is the pay of someone working abroad on a contract of less than a year, such as a Tongan woman on a seven month contract picking fruit in Australia. Her whole pay is counted, whether or not she sends it home, because under the one year rule she still counts as living in Tonga (IMF, n.d., Annex 4).

The figure is built from reports. The banks and the money transfer companies on the screen, the ones your families actually use, tell the central bank how much money they received from abroad and handed over here, and the central bank adds those reports together. MoneyGram and Western Union carry most of the money sent to Tonga and to Jamaica: a survey of Pacific workers put MoneyGram at 54% and Western Union at 20% of transfers on the Australia to Tonga corridor. Remitly and Ria are among the companies priced on the France to Comoros corridor, where Western Union has long been the largest. No household is asked what it received. So the method misses any transfer that does not pass through one of these companies, which we come to after the central bank. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga publishes remittances in four categories, and the pay of Tongans working abroad, seasonal workers among them, is one of them, so you can see that pay separately from money a cousin sends. Watch for that kind of change when you read a series over time: when a central bank starts recording a category separately, or starts capturing something it used to miss, the published total can move without anything changing in the households.

Part one · Demonstration 5 of 9

Why do two official figures for the same remittances disagree?

The remittance tables on boj.org.jm, under Statistics, External Sector
National Reserve Bank of TongaBank of Jamaica, remittancesBanque Centrale des Comores, balance of paymentsRemittances received in US dollars, Tonga
The clicks, in order
  1. Go to your central bank first, because it is the body that produced the number. For Tonga, reservebank.to, menu Economic Reviews, item Remittances, which downloads the bank’s own spreadsheet.
  2. For Jamaica, boj.org.jm, menu Statistics, then External Sector, then Remittances. Four tables download separately: inflows and outflows, by corridor inbound, by corridor outbound, and inflows by parish.
  3. For the Comoros, banque-comores.km, menu Statistiques, item Statistiques de la balance des paiements, and the spreadsheet at the foot of the page.
  4. Then open data.worldbank.org, search Personal remittances, received (current US$), and click your country in the list under the chart, as you did for aid. The line for 2024 reads 253.8 million US dollars.
  5. Read the grey sentence under the title on the World Bank page. It says where its numbers came from.
  6. Write both figures down, the central bank’s own total and the World Bank total, with the year beside each.
What you should see

Personal remittances received in US dollars, World Bank series, latest year each country has.

Tonga, 2024
253.8m
Samoa, 2025
288.1m
Comoros, 2023
305.6m
Jamaica, 2024
3,564.4m

The central bank’s own figure for Tonga, from the spreadsheet in step 1, sheet New Remittances, row 2024, column Total: 524.8 million pa’anga. At the 2024 exchange rate of 2.37 pa’anga to the dollar that is about 221 million US dollars. The World Bank line for the same year reads 253.8 million US dollars.

The same World Bank site publishes aid in US dollars as well, under Net official development assistance received (current US$), so the two flows can be set beside each other in one unit. In 2023, the last year aid is published for all three, families in Tonga were sent 251.9 million US dollars and donors gave 129.5 million; in the Comoros, 305.6 million against 166.4 million; in Jamaica, 3,600.8 million against 86.4 million, about forty times as much (World Bank, n.d.-a; World Bank, n.d.-e).

What this source cannot tell you. Which households received it, or how many of them there are. The whole line is a total for the country, built from what companies reported, and the household survey demonstration is the only source that counts households.

Why this matters

Two bodies published a figure for the same money in the same year and the two do not agree. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga counted 524.8 million pa’anga for 2024, about 221 million US dollars at that year’s rate of 2.37. The World Bank line for 2024 reads 253.8 million US dollars. We cannot tell from these two pages why they differ. The World Bank takes its figure from the IMF balance of payments, and the IMF may include money the central bank does not see in its reports from banks and transfer companies. Both numbers are correct for what each one counts, so you write both down, with the source and the year, and a gap between them is a question for the ministry, not an error to hide.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.-e). Net official development assistance received (current US$) (DT.ODA.ODAT.CD) [Data set]. World Bank Open Data. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.CD

Banque Centrale des Comores. (2023, January 19). Statistiques de la balance des paiements. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://banque-comores.km/page/show/statistiques-de-la-balance-des-paiements

We go to the central bank first, and there is a reason for the order. The central bank is the body that actually counts the money: the banks and money transfer companies in the country report to it what they received from abroad, and it adds those reports together. The World Bank does not repeat that count. It takes the figure through the IMF balance of payments returns, adds its own estimate where a country has not reported, and divides by its own estimate of GDP. The grey line on the World Bank page says exactly that.

I am opening the Tonga central bank now, reservebank.to, and under Economic Reviews you can see Remittances sitting in the menu. Clicking it downloads the bank's own spreadsheet. Open it with me, because this is the step people find hardest, and every central bank file has the same three traps.

First trap, the sheet. This file has three tabs. The one to use is New Remittances, because the note at the foot of it says it follows the current IMF definition, and the tab called Old Remittances stops in 2014. Second trap, the row. The yearly totals sit in the block at the top, one row per year, and the monthly figures below them are only there if you want a month. Find the row 2024. Third trap, the column and the unit. The column called Total gives 524.8, and the line under the title says the unit: million, in the currency of the country, so this is 524.8 million pa’anga, not dollars. There is a fourth trap on this particular sheet. The middle block, Remittances by currency, has a column called USD, and it is not the total in US dollars. It is the part of the money that arrived as US dollars, still written in pa’anga, beside the parts that arrived as Australian and New Zealand dollars, and the four columns add up to the Total. So write down 524.8 million pa’anga as the central bank's figure.

Now put it beside the World Bank line, which is in US dollars. One conversion is all this needs. Divide 524.8 million pa’anga by the year’s average exchange rate, 2.37 pa’anga to the dollar in 2024, which the World Bank publishes as Official exchange rate on the same site, and you have about 221 million US dollars. Now read the World Bank line for 2024 on the page in front of you: 253.8 million US dollars. The same money, the same country, the same year, and about thirty million dollars between the two figures. Before I say anything, tell me why you think two official bodies might publish different totals for the same money. Take a minute with the person next to you.

Here is how far these two pages will take us. We cannot tell from them why they differ. The World Bank takes its figure from the IMF balance of payments, and the IMF may include money the central bank does not see in its reports from banks and transfer companies. Both numbers are correct for what each one counts, so you write both down, with the source and the year, and a gap between them is a question for the ministry, not an error to hide. If your first thought just now was that one of the two must be wrong, that is the habit this module is trying to break.

The rule for any island is short. Find the sheet that follows the current definition, the row for the year, the column called Total or Personal transfers, and the unit line at the top that says the currency and whether the figures are in millions. Every central bank file has those four things, however it is laid out.

The three central banks are three levels of detail, and that is the real lesson of this slide. Tonga publishes a spreadsheet running from 1993 that separates seasonal workers’ earnings from money a relative sends. Jamaica publishes remittances by parish, which is the only sub-national remittance figure any of these three countries has. The Comoros publishes a balance of payments spreadsheet that ends in 2021 and is built on the fifth edition of the IMF manual rather than the sixth. All three are doing the same job with different resources.

Now look at the two flows side by side on the slide, in the same unit and the same year. In 2023 donors gave Tonga 129.5 million US dollars and families were sent 251.9 million, so families sent about twice what donors gave. In the Comoros it was 305.6 million against 166.4 million. In Jamaica it was 3,600.8 million against 86.4 million, about forty times as much (World Bank, n.d.-a; World Bank, n.d.-e).

Now think about where each of those flows is managed. For aid, every one of these governments has somewhere it is handled: a unit in the ministry of finance or in a planning office, staff whose working week is the donor relationship, a line in the budget, a report that goes back to the donor. Name me the office that does the same job for the larger flow. I do not know of one in any of our three countries. The money families send is counted once a year by the central bank, for the balance of payments, and after that no office is responsible for it, because it is private money between relatives that nobody asked the government for. So the smaller flow has a department and the larger one has a statistic. If there is an office on your island that I have missed, I would like to hear about it, because that is the kind of thing I am in this room to learn.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search for your country’s name and the words central bank remittances, and look for the bank’s own address rather than a news article. For the World Bank series search Personal remittances received current US dollars World Bank. If your island is not one of our three, its central bank still publishes a balance of payments, because the IMF requires it. Look for a menu called Statistics, Economic Reviews, Publications or Research. The remittance line may be called personal transfers, workers’ remittances, secondary income or, in French, transferts courants. If the bank publishes only a quarterly report as a PDF, which is common, search that PDF for the word remittance or transfert and take the figure from the table, writing down which quarter it covers.

Part one · What the remittance figure leaves out

What the national remittance figure leaves out

Cash carried by hand

Cash in a suitcase

Money brought home on a visit, or given to a friend who is travelling, never passes through a bank or a transfer company, so nobody reports it.

Goods sent instead of money

The barrel

A barrel of food, a laptop or a pair of school shoes is a real transfer, and no line of the balance of payments records it.

Bills paid from abroad

The school fee

When a relative pays a school fee or a hospital bill directly from abroad, the household never handles the money, so nobody reports it.

A question for you

Who has sent or received something from a relative abroad that was not money in a bank? What was it, and who decided what to send?

Sources

Das, A., Brown, L., McFarlane, A., & Campbell, K. (2021). Remittances and reverse flows in Jamaica. The Journal of Developing Areas, 55(4), 211–233. https://doi.org/10.1353/jda.2021.0087

Before I give you the list, give me your own examples, in the word you use at home. If you are from Jamaica you know the barrel that comes by ship. If you are from Tonga or Samoa you know the box or the parcel that comes back with a relative, and the money collected for a funeral or a church donation. If you are from the Comoros you know cash carried by hand between Marseille and Moroni. Cash carried by hand, in a suitcase on a visit home or given to a friend who is travelling, never passes through a bank. Goods sent instead of money, such as a barrel of food, a laptop or school shoes, are real transfers that no line in the balance of payments records. Bills paid directly from abroad, such as a school fee or a hospital bill settled from Auckland or Miami, never reach the household as money, so the household never reports them.

So the official figure is the smallest amount that households could have received, and the true amount is larger by an amount that nobody knows. The figure also counts the money coming in without subtracting what goes out again. Das and colleagues followed the extra dollar after it reaches Jamaica and found that about 24 cents of it leaves the country again (Das et al., 2021). It leaves in three ways: the government and firms use foreign currency to pay what they owe to lenders abroad, the central bank holds some of it as reserves rather than letting it circulate at home, and some is moved out by people who are able to move money. None of that is the transfer company's fee, which is taken before the money ever reaches the household, and the fee comes in a moment.

Part one · What the transfer costs

The cost of sending money home

The cost is the company’s fee plus the margin it takes on the exchange rate. The bars are averages across the providers surveyed in each corridor.

The target

Under 3% by 2030

Sustainable Development Goal 10 commits governments to bring the cost below 3% and to end corridors above 5%. The world average was 6.36% in the third quarter of 2025.

The same corridor

2.77% or 17.63%

Sending 200 US dollars from New Zealand to Tonga in the third quarter of 2025, the cheapest operator charged 2.77% and a bank branch 17.63%. From Australia the cheapest charged 0.92% and one bank 22.49%. The average hides that choice.

What the target is worth

A$79 million a year

The Lowy Institute estimates that households in Fiji, Tonga and Vanuatu together would keep about this much more each year if their corridors met the 3% target.

Discuss

Should it cost anything to send your own wages home to your family, and if the transfer is digital, why does the price stay this high?

Every figure we have used so far is the money that arrived. Some of what the family sent never arrives, because the company that carries it keeps a part.

Sending 200 US dollars from New Zealand to Tonga cost 7.89% in the third quarter of 2025, and 7.65% from Australia. From the United States to Jamaica it cost 6.06%, and from France to the Comoros 3.78%. The world average was 6.36%. The cost is made of two things: the fee the company charges, and the exchange rate it gives you, which is usually a little worse than the rate on the screen at the bank, and that difference is part of what you pay.

Governments agreed a target on this. Sustainable Development Goal 10 commits countries to bring the cost of sending money home below 3% by 2030, and to end corridors that cost more than 5%. The world is at roughly double the target, and the United Nations reported in 2025 that it had risen rather than fallen the year before.

Two things here are worth arguing about. First, the average hides a wide spread. In the same New Zealand to Tonga corridor, in the third quarter of 2025, the cheapest operator charged 2.77% and a bank branch charged 17.63% to send 200 US dollars, and from Australia the cheapest charged 0.92% and one bank 22.49%, so what a family pays depends on which counter it walks up to and whether it can use a phone. A survey of 1,160 Tongan households found that four in five of the people using the two largest companies had chosen them because they were easy to use, and only two in five gave cost as a reason, while the people who had chosen the cheapest provider were the ones who had paid attention to price (Edwards, Maeda and Suryadarma, 2024). Devpolicy researchers argue from this that the simple average overstates what a careful sender actually pays.

Second, why the price stays high. The reasons are not that the companies are greedy, and there are four of them. I want to take them one at a time, because each is a different kind of problem and each would need a different answer.

The first is the size of the corridor. Almost everything it costs to run a money transfer business is paid whether the corridor carries one million dollars a year or a hundred million: the licence, the staff who check every transaction against the anti-money-laundering rules, the audits, the bank account, the money that has to sit in an account at the receiving end before a single transfer can be paid out, and the shop or the kiosk at each end. That bill is then shared out among the transfers that actually happen. Where there are few transfers, each one carries more of it, and because the price is quoted as a percentage of the amount sent, the percentage is high before anybody has done anything wrong. You can watch the same arithmetic in the World Bank’s own figures for the same quarter: sending 200 US dollars cost 6.36% on average worldwide and sending 500 dollars cost 4.08%, because the fixed part of the charge was spread over a larger transfer (World Bank, 2025a). The World Bank’s Pacific team now proposes pooling the payment volumes of several countries for this reason, because Tuvalu or Kiribati on its own is too small to interest a bank, and Solomon Islands, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea together are not (World Bank, 2025b).

The second is that banks in Australia and New Zealand have been closing the accounts of the companies that carry the money. A money transfer company is not a bank, so it needs a bank account to hold what customers pay in and to move the money across the border. When that account is closed the company cannot trade, whatever else it has. The banks are not usually acting on evidence that anything was wrong. They are weighing the fee income from a small Pacific operator, which is small, against what it costs them to satisfy a regulator that every one of those transfers was clean, and against what one money-laundering case would do to them. AUSTRAC, the Australian financial intelligence regulator, counted at least 719 remittance business accounts closed by banks in Australia between January 2014 and April 2015 (AUSTRAC, n.d.). The word the industry uses for this is de-risking, which means dropping a customer to avoid the cost and the risk of checking them, rather than because they were found to be a problem.

The third follows from the second. When operators lose their bank accounts, some of them stop trading, and the ones that remain have less reason to compete on price. In Tonga, the Nikkei Asian Review reported in 2016 that where there had been roughly one locally owned transfer company for every ten thousand people, by then there were effectively none (Nikkei Asian Review, 2016). On the Australia to Tonga corridor today, MoneyGram and Western Union between them serve about three quarters of the households surveyed, and on that same corridor Ria charged 1.76% while Western Union charged 7.38% for an online transfer (Edwards, Maeda and Suryadarma, 2024). The cheap option is there and most people do not use it.

The fourth is cash. A digital transfer is two changes made in two computer records, and it costs very little to send. A cash transfer is a physical operation. Somebody staffs a counter, holds banknotes on the premises, insures them, restocks them from a bank branch that may be a boat ride away, and takes a commission for doing it, and the company has to keep working balances of pa’anga at every pay-out point, money that sits there earning nothing. The World Bank measured the difference in the same quarter: a transfer paid out in cash cost 5.56% on average against 3.92% paid into a mobile wallet, and services that were not digital averaged 7.30% against 4.59% for the digital ones (World Bank, 2025a). In the Tongan survey, 44 in every hundred households using MoneyGram received the money in cash, which is part of why the price people actually pay stays high even where cheaper channels exist (Edwards, Maeda and Suryadarma, 2024).

Put the four together and you have the Pacific price. The corridors are small, so the fixed bill is shared among few transfers. Because they are small and are scored as risky, banks will not bank them, so operators leave. With fewer operators there is less pressure on price. And because families want cash at the other end, the companies that remain have to carry the most expensive way of delivering it.

So the question on the screen is for you. The Lowy Institute estimates that households in Fiji, Tonga and Vanuatu would keep about 79 million Australian dollars a year more if the 3% target were met, which is larger than some of the aid programmes we will look at this afternoon. Who should carry that cost: the companies, the banks, the sending governments or the families? And as you argue, notice who in that list has the least room to refuse.

The target is under 3% by 2030. The Sustainable Development Goals set it. The France to Comoros corridor comes close to it and the New Zealand to Tonga corridor charges more than twice it, so the poorest corridor is not automatically the most expensive.

What this source cannot tell you. What any particular family actually paid, or whether it used a company on the list at all. Cash carried home by hand appears in none of these tables.

Why this matters

On the New Zealand to Tonga corridor, a family sending 200 US dollars a month pays the cheapest company on the list 5.55 dollars a month in transfer costs, about 67 dollars a year, and pays the most expensive company 35.26 dollars a month, about 423 dollars a year, for exactly the same transfer. The difference, about 357 dollars a year, depends only on which company the sender chooses. If your family sends or receives money, this table shows what the company they use charges beside every other company on the same corridor.

Every figure so far is money that arrived. This site shows what the transfer company took out before it arrived. I am opening remittanceprices.worldbank.org now; open it with me. At the top of the page, choose the country the money is sent from and the country it is sent to, and click Go. The site calls each pair of countries a corridor, so New Zealand to Tonga is one corridor and France to the Comoros is another. I am choosing New Zealand and Tonga.

Above the table, click USD and then 200.00 USD, so that every company is priced for the same transfer of 200 US dollars. Now read the Kiwibank row with me, because the columns catch people out. The Fee column is in dollars: 26.92 dollars on a 200 dollar transfer, which is 13.46%. The Exchange rate margin column is already a percentage, 4.17%. The margin is the difference between the exchange rate the company gives you and the rate at which the two currencies are actually traded, and no company prints it on the receipt. Add the two and you have the Total cost column, 17.63%, and the last column turns that back into money: 35.26 dollars out of the 200. The Total cost column is the only one to compare.

Now look at the spread rather than the average. On this corridor the cheapest company charges 2.77% and the most expensive, a bank at the branch counter, charges 17.63% for the identical transfer. A family sending 200 dollars a month pays the cheapest company 5.55 dollars a month in transfer costs, about 67 dollars a year, and pays the most expensive company 35.26 dollars a month, about 423 dollars a year. The difference is about 357 dollars a year, a term of school fees in Tonga, and it depends only on which counter the sender walks up to. If your family sends or receives money, which company do they use, and has anyone in the family ever compared? Take a moment on that.

One more thing on this site may surprise you. The France to the Comoros corridor, to the poorest of our three countries, is cheaper than the New Zealand to Tonga corridor, and it comes close to the 2030 target of under 3%. The cost of a transfer follows how many companies compete on a route and how many customers use it, not how poor the receiving country is.

If this page has moved by the time you look for it, search Remittance Prices Worldwide and use the Corridors menu at the top of the site. If your island is not one of our three, the site covers only the corridors with the largest flows, so yours may be missing. If it is, say so in your map, then look for the nearest comparable corridor from the same sending country and label it as a substitute. Never quote a corridor you did not check as though it were yours.

Why this matters

For every 100 people living in Tonga, 51 people born in Tonga live abroad. For Jamaica the figure is 44 for every 100 at home, and for the Comoros 42. The central bank demonstration gave you the money that families send home. This slide gives you the people who send it, and it takes two minutes once you know where the numbers are. I am opening un.org/development/desa/pd; choose Data in the top menu, then International Migrant Stock. On the right of the page, under Data, click Total, origin. Origin means the country a person was born in, so this file counts people born in Tonga wherever they live now. A spreadsheet downloads; open the sheet called Table 1.

Now the part where you might get confused, because I did. Find your country’s row, and before you read anything look at the headings at the top of the sheet. The years 1990 to 2024 run three times across the page: the first block is both sexes together, the second is men, the third is women, and the heading that says which block you are in sits two rows above the years, so once you scroll to the right you see only a year. If you go straight to the last column you get the women’s figure and think it is the total. Go back to the first column headed 2024 for the total. For Tonga: 53,237 people abroad in 2024, of whom 28,839 are men and 24,398 are women.

That number means little on its own, so we need the number living at home, and it is on the site you already know. Open data.worldbank.org, type Population, total, click the line with that name, and click Tonga in the list under the chart: 104,175 people in 2024. Put the two together: for every 100 people living in Tonga, 51 people born in Tonga live abroad. For Jamaica it is 44 for every 100, and for the Comoros 42. The remittance figure from the central bank is sent by this group, so when a ministry reads that Tonga’s remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024 (World Bank, n.d.-b), this is the size of the population behind that number.

Now the men and the women. From Tonga, more men are abroad than women, 28,839 against 24,398, and the seasonal work schemes in Australia and New Zealand, which recruit mostly men for fruit picking and meat packing, are part of the reason; we come back to those schemes this afternoon. From Jamaica and the Comoros, more women are abroad than men. Why should a ministry care which it is? Think about it for a moment. Here are two reasons to start with. Who is abroad decides who is missing at home: a village where the men are away has women running the farms and the households, and a village where the women are away has grandmothers raising the children. And the schemes that send men abroad are government policy, so a ministry that sees men leaving in their thousands is looking at the result of its own agreements.

What this file cannot tell you is who among the 53,237 sends money and who does not, or what the money pays for once it arrives. The count is of people abroad, not of senders. No national figure goes that far, which is why the FAR-SIDS household survey asks each household how many women and how many men outside the house sent money or goods in the last year, and who in the house received it. Write your four numbers down with their year, and keep them beside the remittance figure.

Part one · How the survey question changes the figure

How many households receive remittances depends on how you ask it

Each bar is the share of Tongan households that had received money from relatives in the year before they were asked. The 2001 and 2021 counts come from Tonga’s national household surveys, which asked about cash only. The 2004 count comes from Brown and Leeves, who surveyed 500 Tongan households and asked about goods, school fees and bills paid for the household as well as cash.

What the three counts showIn 2001 the national survey asked one question about cash, and 75 in every hundred Tongan households said they had received money from abroad in the previous year. In 2004 Brown and Leeves asked many questions, covering money, goods, school fees and bills paid for the household, and 90 in every hundred had received something. In 2021 the national survey asked the single cash question again and also found 90 in every hundred, so more households really were receiving money than in 2001.
Who receives, 2021Of every hundred Tongan households headed by a woman, 96 received cash from relatives in the previous twelve months. Of every hundred headed by a man, 88 did. A third of that money was sent from New Zealand and a third from Australia.
Households with nobody abroad, 200433 in every hundred Tongan households had no family member living abroad and still received money from relatives overseas, because money travels along family networks beyond the house the migrant left.
Sources

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

Tonga Statistics Department. (2022). Tonga 2021 household income and expenditure survey report. https://tongastats.gov.to/download/47/household-income-expenditure-survey/8078/tonga-2021-hies-report.pdf

In a household survey, a statistics office visits a sample of households, asks the same questions in every house, and publishes the answers as figures for the whole country. It is the only source that counts households rather than dollars, and what it finds depends on the wording of the question.

Tonga has three of these counts. The national survey of 2001 asked one general question about cash sent from abroad, and 75 in every hundred households said yes. Three years later two economists, Richard Brown and Gareth Leeves, surveyed 500 Tongan households about what they had received during 2004, and they asked many questions instead of one: money sent, goods sent, school fees paid for the household, bills settled from abroad, and transfers that people do not think of as remittances at all. Ninety in every hundred households had received something (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 2 on p. 3968). The two surveys are three years apart and fifteen households in a hundred apart, and the authors put almost all of that gap down to the questions rather than to any change in Tongan families.

Then the national survey of 2021 asked the narrow question again, about cash received in the last twelve months, and this time 90 in every hundred households said yes (Tonga Statistics Department, 2022, pp. 21 and 22, Figure 37). The narrow question in 2021 found what only the detailed questionnaire had found in 2004, so between 2001 and 2021 the number of households receiving cash from relatives really did rise, and receiving has become close to universal.

The 2021 survey also reports who receives. Of every hundred households headed by a woman, 96 received cash, against 88 of every hundred headed by a man, and a third of the money came from New Zealand and a third from Australia. The 2004 survey adds one more finding that matters for tomorrow: 33 in every hundred households had nobody living abroad and still received money, because it travels along family networks beyond the house the migrant left. More households receive than have a migrant of their own.

So before you compare two years, or two countries, find the question each survey asked. Two numbers that look like the same measure are often answers to different questions.

And no survey anywhere gives the matching figure for aid: there is no national count of households that received an aid programme.

Why this matters

This is the only figure in the whole day that counts households rather than dollars. For remittances it tells you how many households receive and which kinds: in Tonga nine in every ten, in Jamaica just over half, and in all three countries the better off households more often than the poorest. For aid there is no such figure anywhere, because donors count money paid and projects built, never the households a programme reached. Tomorrow’s map asks who was left out of each flow, and this slide is the last source that can answer any part of it; the rest you fill from what you know about your own island.
