Every source so far counts money crossing a border. This one counts households, and it is the only source in the day that does. Your assignment asks who receives and who decides, and it cannot begin without this figure.

I am doing it for Tonga; follow on your own laptop. Open tongastats.gov.to, choose Survey in the top menu, then Household Income and Expenditure Survey, scroll to HIES reports and click Download beside Tonga 2021 HIES Report. The file is 149 pages, and you need one of them. Search the PDF for the word remittance. The first hits are the contents pages; keep going to the first hit in the text itself, which is printed page 21, section 1.2.3, one paragraph. It says that 90% of households received cash remittances in the twelve months before the survey, that the highest shares were in Vava’u and rural Tongatapu and the lowest in Ongo Niua at 64%, and that 96% of households headed by a woman received against 88% headed by a man. Turn the page and Figure 37 gives the same 90% split every way the survey can split it: by island, by town and country, by the sex and the age of the head, by disability, and by the five spending groups from poorest to richest, where the poorest fifth is at 87% and the richest at 90%. The year the survey was in the field, January to November 2021, is on page xi.

Now the third thing to write down: the report’s own words for what it counted. Here they are “cash remittances during the last 12 months”. Nothing in that says from abroad. Figure 38 on page 22 confirms it: about a third of the money came from New Zealand, a third from Australia, and the rest from the United States, from elsewhere, and from inside Tonga, and households in Ongo Niua depended mostly on cash from other islands. So Tonga’s 90% is households receiving cash from anyone outside the house, at home or overseas. A student who writes “90% of Tongan households receive remittances from abroad” has misread the report. That is why you copy the words and not just the number, and it is the lesson of the three surveys slide earlier this afternoon.

Your island may not publish a report like this, or may publish it differently. Here are two of our own three. Jamaica sells its full survey report for 30 dollars, but the ten page overview is free on the Planning Institute’s site, and the figure is on its page xii: 55.9% of households received remittances in 2019, 63.6% in Kingston and 48.3% in the other towns, 42.5% of the poorest fifth of households against 61.0% of the richest, 59.4% of households headed by a woman against 53.1% headed by a man. The Comoros published a 17 page results report for its 2024 survey in May this year, in French, on the statistics office’s own data catalogue. It gives no single national share. Instead, its Figure 7 gives the share of people receiving money from abroad for each tenth of households from poorest to richest, and the text on page 10 says the richest households are about 15 percentage points more likely to receive than the poorest, and that the richest tenth of households receive about a quarter of all the money sent from abroad. So for the Comoros you write down the figure by spending group, say that the report gives no national total, and cite the page.

Put the three beside each other and one pattern appears in all of them. In Tonga money from abroad makes up 22% of income in the poorest fifth of households and 40% in the richest fifth. In Jamaica 42.5% of the poorest fifth receive against 61.0% of the richest. In the Comoros the richest tenth receive a quarter of the money. In every one of our three countries the better off households receive more, not less. Most people expect the opposite, so sit with two questions. First: if the poorest households receive the least from abroad, who is remittance money a safety net for, and who is left without one? Second: aid programmes usually choose their households by a rule, the poorest, the most exposed to cyclones, the ones without a water tank, while remittances arrive with a person and go where that person’s family is. Do the two flows reach the same households, or different ones? No survey in the world answers that today, because no survey asks about aid and remittances in the same house, and that is the question the FAR-SIDS household survey is built to ask.

What this report cannot tell you is how much each household received, who inside the house received it, or who decided what to do with it. And for aid there is no report like this anywhere: donors count money paid and projects built, and no statistics office counts the households an aid programme reached. Tomorrow’s map asks who was left out of each flow, and after this slide you have every public source there is for it. The rest of that box you fill from what you know about your own island, which is the point of the map.

Part one · What you can now find, and what no figure says

Part one on one page: what you can now find, and what no figure says

You can now find
  • How much aid arrived and who paid it: the World Bank page and the OECD table, with AidData and the Lowy map for China.
  • How much money families were sent: your central bank and the World Bank, and what the transfer cost on your corridor.
  • How many people are abroad, and how many households receive: the United Nations count and your own statistics office’s survey.
What each figure leaves out
  • Aid: donors that report to nobody, money promised but not paid, and every household a project reached.
  • Remittances: cash carried by hand, goods sent instead of money, bills paid from abroad, and the fee taken before the money arrives.
  • Every figure: who received the money, who decided what it was for, and what the household gave up to get it.
Write beside every figure
  • What it measures: gross aid is what arrived, net aid subtracts what was repaid; the OECD reports gross and the World Bank net.
  • What it is divided by: aid shares by GNI, remittance shares by GDP. Say which.
  • The year and the source. Tonga’s net aid was 50.7% of national income in 2022, the eruption year, and 20.3% in 2023; one year is one point.
Part two

Part two asks what happens once the money has arrived: who decides what a dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance are for, and why the two are used differently inside the same house.

That closes part one, so here it is on one page. You can now find, for any island, how much aid arrived and who paid it, from the World Bank page and the OECD table, with AidData and the Lowy map for the money China does not report. You can find how much money families were sent, from your central bank and from the World Bank, and what the transfer cost on your corridor. And you can find how many people from your island are abroad, from the United Nations count, and how many households receive, from your own statistics office’s survey. That is nine websites, and you have seen every one of them opened.

You have also seen what each figure leaves out. The aid figure leaves out donors that report to nobody, money promised and not yet paid, and every household a project reached, because no database counts households. The remittance figure leaves out cash carried by hand, goods sent instead of money, bills paid directly from abroad, and the fee the company took before the money arrived. And every figure, both of them, leaves out who received the money, who decided what it was for, and what the household gave up to get it. Those three are the question of the week, and no figure in part one answers them.

So the rule for every figure in your classwork and your assignment: beside it, write what it measures, the year, and where you found it. What it measures matters because the two largest databases use different rules. Gross aid counts what arrived, which was 150.9 million US dollars for Tonga in 2024 in the OECD database, while net aid subtracts what Tonga repaid that year on earlier aid loans, which was 129.5 million in 2023 in the World Bank series. Aid shares are usually divided by GNI, gross national income, which starts from GDP, adds what residents earn abroad and subtracts what foreigners earn inside the country, whereas remittance shares are usually divided by GDP; in an economy that depends on remittances the two totals differ, so say which one you used. And a figure needs its year. Tonga’s net aid was 50.7% of national income in 2022 and 20.3% in 2023, and both are right: in January 2022 the Hunga Tonga volcano erupted and donors paid for the repairs, so one year tells you where a country stood at one moment, and several years tell you whether that moment was ordinary.

Part two asks what happens once the money has arrived: who decides what a dollar of aid and a dollar of remittance are for, and why the two are used differently inside the same house.

Part two

Who decides what the money is for

A dollar of aid and a dollar sent by a relative are the same money at the bank. Inside the household they are not, because different people decided what each one was for. Tonga is the worked example.

Who decides

The usual path each kind of money takes to a household, where the two paths differ, and the case where a government sits at the top of both.

What researchers find

When the two flows are compared in the same study they behave differently, in the economy and in the household, and the same flow behaves differently from one place to another.

Tonga in both accounts

The same country read from the national accounts, and then read from the household.

We have spent the first part of the afternoon on how the money is counted. Now we ask what happens once it has arrived. At the bank, a dollar of aid and a dollar sent by a sister in Auckland are identical. Inside an island they are not, and the reason is that different people decide what each dollar is for, and they decide from different places, under different conditions.

By different conditions I mean who chose the purpose, what the money can become once it is here, and what the receiver owes in return. An aid agency in Canberra or Brussels usually writes down what a grant is for before your government has seen it, whereas a sister in Auckland decides on the phone on a Sunday night, often with the household on the other end of the call. A water tank paid for by a donor stays a water tank, and it is very hard to turn it into school fees, whereas cash from a sister can become school fees on Monday and a roof repair after the next cyclone. An aid project usually asks your government for reports, audits and conditions, whereas a remittance carries obligations to the sender, to the church and to the family that no ministry can see, because they are never written down.

Before we go further, think about your own household. Think of the last money that came into it from outside: a wage, a scholarship, a government payment, a transfer from a relative. Who decided what it was for, and where was that person when they decided? Keep your answer, because I will ask you for it in a few minutes.

Tonga is the example I use through this part of the session, because Tonga receives both kinds of money on a large scale, and because the data allow us to look at the same country from the national accounts and from inside the household.

Part two · Who decides

The distance between the decision and the household

The shaded steps are where the household enters. In the aid path the decisions are recorded in documents and made a long way from the household. In the remittance path they are made between family members and recorded nowhere a ministry can read, which is why a household survey, and not the national accounts, is where you learn what a remittance was for.

A question for you

At which step of the aid path does anybody ask the household what it needs? In your own family, who has the last word on what a remittance is for, the person who sent it or the person who received it? And if a programme started paying your school fees tomorrow, and your sister abroad kept sending the same amount, where would that money go: to something else inside the house, or to the church and the family events?

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Remittance Prices Worldwide: New Zealand to Tonga [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://remittanceprices.worldbank.org/corridor/New-Zealand/Tonga

The two paths on the screen are one common case each, and I want you to treat them as examples rather than as rules. In the aid path, a donor parliament in Canberra, Wellington or Brussels votes the budget, the aid agency chooses countries and sectors, your government negotiates the project and often puts in money of its own, the project team writes the rule for who takes part, some households fit the rule and some do not, and the household that fits usually receives a service rather than cash: a tank, a clinic, a fee waiver, or in a growing number of programmes a payment with a condition attached, such as keeping a child in school.

That is a project, and aid does not always arrive as a project. When a donor gives budget support, the money goes straight into your government's general budget, there is no project team and no selection rule, and the household never knows which road or which nurse the donor paid for. When aid arrives as a scholarship, the household is chosen by an exam and receives something close to cash. When it arrives after a cyclone, the negotiation is skipped, the money comes in weeks, and it comes as tarpaulins and rice. So the six steps are the usual path for a project, and the number of steps can be four or eight depending on the form the aid takes.

Now the remittance path. A relative abroad earns the money and decides how much to send and what for, and I say decides with the household because in most families I know that decision is a phone call, not an order. The money travels, and on the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide series the transfer company took about 8 dollars in every 100 on the New Zealand to Tonga corridor in late 2025. Then the household receives it, and sender and receiver settle between them what it pays for.

That too is one case. The sender is not always abroad; a brother in Nuku’alofa sending money to Ha’apai is a remittance to that household, and it never appears in the national figure. The money does not always pass through a company; a seasonal worker who flies home in October with cash in his bag has remitted, and the national accounts never see it. And the household does not always decide: when a sister sends money marked for the school fee, or pays the school directly, or sends the misinale contribution for the church, the purpose was fixed before the money arrived.

So a remittance can arrive with its purpose already settled, and the person who settled it is not always the sender or the person who receives it.

So, the first question. At which step of the aid path does anybody ask the household what it needs? Look at the chain and find it. In many projects the honest answer is the fourth step at the earliest, when the selection rule is written, and in some projects the answer is nowhere. Now the second question, and I want real answers from your own families. Who has the last word on what a remittance is for, the person who sent it or the person who received it? And does the answer change when the amount is large, when it is a roof rather than a phone top-up?

Now a third question. A programme starts paying a household's school fees. The daughter abroad keeps sending the same amount. The fee is already covered, so where does her money go?

One answer is that it stays in the house and pays for something else the household needs. Researchers call that reallocation within the household, and it answers a relational obligation, which is what she owes the people she is related to.

The other answer is that it goes out again, to the church and to the weddings and funerals the family contributes to. That is redirection to the community, and it answers a cultural obligation, which is what the household owes inside the ceremonial economy.

Two studies have watched this happen, and they point in opposite directions. We come to both of them this afternoon. Tell me which one you would expect in your own family.

Part two · When a government decides the remittance too

How do donor governments and receiving governments influence the flow of remittances?

20,750

places a year

New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, capped at this number since August 2024.

3,715

Tongans working in Australia on seasonal visas

On 30 June 2026, under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme (PALM), 3,095 of them men. On the same day 798 Tongans held New Zealand seasonal work visas, 729 of them men; the New Zealand season peaks in March, when 1,311 held them.

1 in 5

working Tongan men

In a story about Tongans who used their seasonal earnings to open businesses at home, 1News (2 August 2026) put the two schemes together at about 20% of working Tongan men. No official count of that share exists, so the figure is the journalist's.

Does seasonal work count as aid?

Only a small part of it. For New Zealand’s scheme, the OECD counts the training the workers receive as aid and not the cost of running the scheme, because the scheme exists to fill jobs in New Zealand. For Australia’s scheme, it counts only the part paid from the aid budget, which pays for the workers’ skills and support. Workers sending money home is not, by itself, enough to make a scheme aid (OECD DAC, 2023). So a government designs the scheme, the scheme produces the remittances, and the remittances are counted as private money.

Sources

OECD Development Assistance Committee. (2023). ODA casebook on activities in the field of migration (DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL). OECD. https://one.oecd.org/document/DCD/DAC/STAT(2023)34/FINAL/en/pdf

New Zealand Government. (2024, August 14). RSE scheme revitalised and cap increased [Press release]. https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/rse-scheme-revitalised-and-cap-increased

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. (2026). Migration data explorer: Visa holder population by nationality and visa type [Data set]. Retrieved September 17, 2026, from https://www.mbie.govt.nz/immigration-and-tourism/immigration/migration-research-and-evaluation/migration-data-explorer

1News. (2026, August 2). Seasonal work in NZ helping Tongans build businesses back home. https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/02/seasonal-work-in-nz-helping-tongans-build-businesses-back-home/

On the last slide one path had a government at the top and the other had a family. In the Pacific, one of the largest remittance flows has a government at the top as well. Wellington sets the number of places, a Tongan worker earns the money, his family receives it, and the central bank counts it as a private transfer. Labour schemes are where the two kinds of money meet. New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, capped at 20,750 places a year since August 2024, and Australia's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, known as PALM, bring Pacific workers to seasonal jobs such as picking fruit and packing meat, and they produce a large remittance flow by design. On 30 June 2026, 3,715 Tongans held PALM visas in Australia, 3,095 of them men, and on the same day 798 Tongans held New Zealand seasonal work visas, 729 of them men; New Zealand's season peaks in March, when 1,311 Tongans held them (MBIE, 2026). Both figures count people holding a visa on one day, so they can stand side by side. A journalist estimates that the two schemes together employ about one in five working Tongan men, and the screen shows that figure as an estimate.

A donor government therefore designs a labour scheme, the scheme produces remittances, and the remittances are counted as private transfers. The OECD has ruled on both schemes in its casebook. For the New Zealand scheme it counts the workers’ training programme as aid and excludes the cost of running the scheme, because employers must first show that they cannot fill the job locally, so the scheme is there to fill labour shortages in New Zealand. For the Australian scheme it counts the part the aid ministry pays for, and it states that migrants sending money home is not on its own enough to make a programme aid (OECD DAC, 2023). So the schemes are immigration policy with a small aid component, and they produce a private flow that barely appears in the aid statistics of the country that designed them. Jamaica has its own example, the Overseas Employment Programme, which sends workers to Canada and the United States.

Since 2014 Tonga’s central bank has published the pay of seasonal workers as its own line inside the remittance figure, and by 2025 that line was about one tenth of all remittances, so this is one flow you can see on its own. For tomorrow, ask which of your island’s remittance flows exist because of an agreement between two governments, and which would stop if that agreement ended.

Part two · Demonstration 9 of 9

Behind one line of the aid total, who was the money for?

The project list for Jamaica on projects.worldbank.org
World Bank projects, JamaicaWorld Bank projects, all countriesAsian Development Bank projectsInter-American Development Bank projects
The clicks, in order
  1. Open projects.worldbank.org and click the Project List tab.
  2. Open Country in the filter panel on the left, choose your country and click Go.
  3. The table gives the project title, the identifier beginning with P, the commitment amount, the status and the approval date. Open a project whose title looks relevant to a livelihood: housing, social protection, water, schools.
  4. Inside the project, click the Documents tab.
  5. Open the Project Appraisal Document, written before the money is spent. It states who the project is for and how many people it should reach.
  6. Open the Implementation Completion Report, written afterwards, which says how many it actually reached. Its first page carries the grade the lender gives its own project, on a six point scale from highly unsatisfactory to highly satisfactory. For a project funded elsewhere, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank publish the same two documents.
What you should see

Jamaica has 161 World Bank projects listed. The most recent is the Hurricane Melissa Reconstruction Implementation Support Project, P515022, five million US dollars, approved 30 June 2026.

Tonga’s largest current project is the Sustainable Economic Corridors and Urban Resilience Project, P512750: an 80 million US dollar grant from the Asian Development Bank, a 40 million World Bank grant and 25 million from the Government of Tonga, for a bridge across the Fanga’uta lagoon with roads and drainage in Nuku’alofa.

The appraisal document is the only document in the whole day that names a target group, and even it names a number of people rather than a household.

What this source cannot tell you. Whether the people named as the target were the people reached. The completion report gives a count, and no document here follows a single household.

Why this matters

Every aid figure today counted money at the level of the country. These two documents, the appraisal document before the money is spent and the completion report after, are the only ones in the day that name the people a project was meant to reach and how many it reached. For the teal lines of tomorrow’s map, this is where you read who a programme was for, and it is the closest any aid source comes to the answer the household survey gives you for remittances, who receives.

Read that grade with care. Wood, Otor and Dornan (2022) put nine donors’ own grades for 8,062 projects on one scale: Pacific projects came out about 0.15 lower, governance in the Pacific was better than average, and the gap disappeared once remoteness and small population were allowed for, neither of which a country can change. A low grade on a Pacific project partly measures where the island is, so when you quote one in your assignment, say whose measurement it is.

Sources

World Bank. (n.d.). Projects & Operations. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://projects.worldbank.org/

Asian Development Bank. (n.d.). Projects. Retrieved September 18, 2026, from https://www.adb.org/projects

Wood, T., Otor, S., & Dornan, M. (2022). Why are aid projects less effective in the Pacific? Development Policy Review, 40(3), Article e12573. https://doi.org/10.1111/dpr.12573

Two slides ago you saw where the decisions sit on both paths, and the aid path had a step where a project team writes the rule for who takes part. The only public document that says who an aid project was meant to reach, and how many it reached, is the lender's own project document, and this demonstration shows where it lives. I am opening the World Bank project list for Jamaica, then the Hurricane Melissa reconstruction project, and going straight to the Documents tab, so you can see the appraisal document and the completion report sitting side by side.

Most of you have never seen one of these documents, so here is what they are. Before a lender releases money it writes an appraisal document, which argues why the project is needed, states who it is for, and commits to a number of people it will reach. Years later it writes a completion report, which says what happened. Both are public, both are long, and almost nobody outside the institution reads them.

These are the only documents in today’s whole list that name a group of people. Every figure we opened in part one counts dollars crossing a border, and this is where the fourth step of the aid path, the rule for who takes part, is written down.

You do not read the whole document. The appraisal document has a results framework near the front, usually a table, giving the indicators and the target numbers. The completion report has the same table with the achieved column filled in. Those two tables are the five minutes of reading that matter.

One more thing about the completion report. Its first page carries a grade: the lender marks its own project on a six point scale, from highly unsatisfactory to highly satisfactory, on whether it did what the appraisal document promised. Wood, Otor and Dornan (2022) put nine donors’ grades for 8,062 of their own projects onto one scale from 1 to 6. Pacific projects scored about 0.15 lower, and because the grades bunch tightly around 4.25, a Pacific project is more than ten percentage points more likely to come in below its own donor’s average. Governance in the Pacific was better than the developing world average, not worse. Remoteness and small population accounted for the gap, and neither is something a country can change. So a project in Kiribati graded lower partly because Kiribati is far away and small, and when you quote an effectiveness score in your assignment, ask whose measurement you are quoting.

In your group, find one project on your own island and say, from its appraisal document, who the project names as its beneficiaries and whether a household like yours would be among them.

If a page has moved by the time you look, search World Bank projects and operations and use the Project List tab, then the Country filter. If your island is not one of our three, find out which bank lends to it and go to that bank’s project pages. The Asian Development Bank covers the Pacific, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Caribbean Development Bank cover the Caribbean, and the African Development Bank covers the Indian Ocean and Atlantic islands. All four publish appraisal and completion documents under the same two names.

Part two · What researchers find when they compare the two flows

Where and when a study is done decides what it finds

The first of two results from the few studies that hold both flows: what each flow does to prices.

Where the study was doneWhat aid did to pricesWhat remittances did to prices
Nineteen small island statesAmuedo-Dorantes, Pozo and Vargas-Silva, 2007raised pricesno measured change
Thirteen Latin American countriesAmuedo-Dorantes and Pozo, 2004not studiedraised prices
A large sample of countriesRajan and Subramanian, 2011raised prices, and exports grew more slowlynot studied
The real exchange rate, and Dutch diseaseThe price of what your island produces compared with the same goods abroad. A large aid project brings US dollars to Tonga; spent as pa'anga they chase the same builders, drivers and land, so prices and wages rise and the pa'anga strengthens. A squash farmer selling to Japan now has higher costs at home and a dearer price abroad. Economists call that Dutch disease, after the Netherlands in the 1960s.
Why the place mattersIn the island study, families spent remittances mostly on imported goods, which are paid for abroad and give no work to local builders. In Latin America more of the money went to housing and services made at home, which do. A small island produces a narrow range of goods and imports most of what it uses (Briguglio, 1995), and shipping and insurance take about 22% of the value of those imports, against about 15% worldwide (UNCTAD, 2021).
A question for you

If your government receives 50 million next year for a new hospital, and families on your island receive 50 million from relatives in the same year, which of the two would you expect to raise the wage of a builder in your capital, and why?

Why this matters

Two studies of the same thing reached opposite answers because they were done in different places. If you carry a finding from one island to another without asking what that island makes, how far it is from its suppliers and how many people work in the trade the money lands on, you will get the answer wrong in your own country. The question for your assignment is not which flow is better. It is which parts of your own economy each flow actually reaches.

Sources

Amuedo-Dorantes, C., Pozo, S., & Vargas-Silva, C. (2007). Remittances and the macroeconomy: The case of small island developing states (WIDER Research Paper No. 2007/22). UNU-WIDER. https://www.wider.unu.edu/sites/default/files/rp2007-22.pdf

Rajan, R. G., & Subramanian, A. (2011). Aid, Dutch disease, and manufacturing growth. Journal of Development Economics, 94(1), 106–118. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2009.12.004

We have followed each kind of money to the household. Now I want to show you what happens when researchers put the two flows side by side, first in the economy as a whole, on this slide and the next, and then inside the house. Very few studies do this. Most study one flow and treat the other as background, so the results I am about to show you come from a handful of papers, and I will tell you where each one was done, because the place turns out to matter.

The first result is about prices, and the measure is the real exchange rate: the price of what your island produces compared with the price of the same goods abroad. Let me explain it with an example. A large aid project arrives in Tonga and brings US dollars. To spend them in Tonga, the dollars have to be changed into pa'anga and spent on Tongan things: builders, drivers, office staff, land, rent. The island has only so many builders and so much land, so when a lot of new money chases the same builders and the same plots, their prices and wages go up. At the same time, all those dollars being changed into pa'anga make the pa'anga stronger. Now think of a farmer who sells squash to Japan, or a hotel that sells rooms to Australians. Their costs at home have gone up, and a foreign buyer needs more dollars to pay the same price in pa'anga, so their squash and their rooms have become dearer abroad and they sell less. Economists call this Dutch disease, after what happened in the Netherlands when income from natural gas arrived in the 1960s.

Now look at the rows. Across nineteen small island states, aid raised the real exchange rate and remittances produced no measurable change (Amuedo-Dorantes, Pozo and Vargas-Silva, 2007). If I stopped there, you would leave thinking that remittances are harmless and aid is not. Across thirteen Latin American countries remittances did raise it (Amuedo-Dorantes and Pozo, 2004), and across a much larger sample aid raised it and export industries grew more slowly (Rajan and Subramanian, 2011). The same flow, opposite results, in different places.

The explanation the authors give is the composition of expenditure. In the island sample, remittances were spent largely on imported goods, which are paid for abroad and place no demand on domestic builders, land or wages. In Latin America a larger share went to housing and services produced at home, and those do create work for local builders and push local wages up.

I want to take that one step further, because stated as a difference in what families bought it reads as a difference in preference. It is also a difference in what the two economies produce. This argument has a Maltese history, and you are sitting in the building where it was developed. In 1990 Malta's ambassador to the United Nations put it to an UNCTAD meeting that GDP per person on its own does not measure the development of island states, because it does not reflect their structural handicaps. Lino Briguglio, at this institute, set those handicaps out five years later and built the first index of them (Briguglio, 1995; UNCTAD, 2021).

Three of the characteristics he identified bear on this directly. Small island economies have limited natural resource endowments and low interindustry linkages, which means that domestic industries buy little from one another, so demand leaks out of the economy as imports. They have a limited ability to exploit economies of scale, because a small domestic market does not support production at a viable scale. And they are remote, so whatever is not produced at home arrives by sea (Briguglio, 1995).

The figures follow from that. Trade, exports plus imports, averaged 95% of GDP across small island developing states between 2005 and 2019, against 65% for developing countries as a whole. Bringing goods in by sea, the freight and the insurance of the cargo against loss on the way, takes about 22% of the value of what those states import, against a world average of about 15%, so the same dollar buys less of the good itself. Food alone is more than 15% of their import bill, against a world average of 8.4% (UNCTAD, 2021). Tonga has imported the equivalent of between 57% and 66% of its GDP in every year since 2018, and 60.7% in 2024 (World Bank, n.d.). That is a structural feature of the economy, not a shock.

So when a Tongan household spends a remittance on a fridge, a motorbike or rice, it is choosing from a narrow domestic production base. A household in Bogotá buying cement and paying a builder is choosing from a wider one. The conclusion is not that one flow is benign and the other harmful. The effect on the real exchange rate depends on who spends the money, on what, and on how much of what they buy is produced at home, and that last term is a property of the economy rather than of the household.

So here is my question, and I want you to answer it for your own island. If your government receives 50 million next year for a new hospital, and families on your island receive 50 million from relatives in the same year, which of the two would you expect to raise the wage of a builder in your capital, and why? Think about who spends each 50 million and what they spend it on. Talk to the person beside you for two minutes and then I want answers.

If nobody wants to start, here are four things to argue with, and you can disagree with all of them. The first is how the money lands. The hospital money is spent in one place, over about two years, by one buyer, on construction, so it reaches a small number of builders at once. The 50 million from families arrives in small amounts, across thousands of households, through the whole year, and it is spread over food, school fees, fares, a funeral and a roof. How the money is concentrated may matter as much as how much of it there is. The second is what your island makes. If the cement, the timber and the roofing all arrive by ship, a large part of both 50 millions leaves again as soon as it is spent, and neither one bids up a wage at home. If your island has quarries, sawmills and a construction industry, both of them do. The third is how many builders there are. Where a country has a few hundred qualified builders, either sum can take up the whole trade and wages move; in a labour market the size of Kingston’s, neither would be noticed. The fourth is who decides and under what rules. If the donor brings its own contractor, some of those wages are paid to people who are not on your island at all, and then procurement rules, and where the ministry chooses to build, decide more than the size of the cheque does. Now give me your answer, and tell me which of the four you are leaning on.

Part two · What researchers find when they compare the two flows

Does aid cause the outcome, or does the outcome attract the aid?

The second result: what aid is spent on, and the problem that had to be solved before anyone could measure it.

The problem · endogeneity

Aid is not handed out at random

It goes to countries that are poor, that have just been hit by something, or that a donor favours. So when a researcher finds more aid and more poverty in the same country, the aid may have caused the poverty or the poverty may have attracted the aid. Economists call this endogeneity: the thing you want to measure is itself shaped by the outcome you measure it against.

The fix · a natural experiment

Let something outside the country move the aid

Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait earn more when the world oil price rises, and when it did they gave more to poorer countries with Muslim majorities. Nothing Bangladesh, Mali or the Comoros did set that price, so the extra aid arrived as if by chance. The oil price is the instrumental variable: it moves the aid and cannot reach the household by any other route (Werker, Ahmed and Cohen, 2009).

What they found

Consumption and imports rose, saving fell

For each extra 1% of national output received as aid, household consumption rose by at least 0.6% of output and imports by about 1%, while domestic saving fell by close to the value of the aid (Werker et al., 2009, p. 227). And once the remittances that rose in the same years were counted, the measured effect of aid fell by up to a third (Werker et al., 2009, p. 240).

A question for you

Think of the aid your island received after its last cyclone. It came because of the damage. So when a researcher finds more aid and more hardship in the same year, which is the cause and which is the effect, and how would you tell?

Why this matters

A study that measures one flow and leaves out the other credits the first with what the second paid for. Remittances rose in the same years as the Gulf aid, and counting them took up to a third off what had looked like the effect of aid. That is why FAR-SIDS looks at aid and remittances in the same household, and why your assignment asks about both flows.

Sources

Werker, E., Ahmed, F. Z., & Cohen, C. (2009). How is foreign aid spent? Evidence from a natural experiment. American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, 1(2), 225–244. https://doi.org/10.1257/mac.1.2.225

The second result is about what aid is spent on once it arrives, and about a problem that had to be solved before anyone could measure it. The problem has a name in economics, endogeneity, and so does the solution, an instrumental variable. I will explain both through the study itself, with the drawing on the screen.

The problem is this. Aid is not allocated at random. It goes to countries that are poor, that have just been hit by something, or that a donor has its own reasons to favour. So when a researcher finds aid and a poor outcome in the same country, the aid may have produced the outcome, or the outcome may have attracted the aid. Nothing in the data separates the two. Economists call this endogeneity: the amount of aid a country receives is not independent of the outcome you want to measure it against, so the arrow on the left of the screen could point either way.

Werker, Ahmed and Cohen (2009) found a case where that problem does not arise. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait earn more when the world oil price rises, and when they did, they gave more to poorer countries with Muslim majorities. The oil price is set on world markets, so the amount that arrived in Bangladesh, Mali or the Comoros in a given year was not settled by anything those countries did or failed to do. The money also arrived as unconditional grants to finance ministries rather than as projects (Werker et al., 2009, p. 226), so there is no project spending to separate from ordinary government spending. That gives them a clean comparison: set those countries beside other poor countries in the same year, and attribute the difference to the aid. The oil price is what economists call an instrumental variable: something that moves the aid, and that cannot reach household consumption in Bangladesh by any route other than the aid. That is the whole trick, and it is why this study can say cause where most studies can only say association.

What they found. For each additional 1% of national output received as aid, household consumption rose by at least 0.6% of output, and imports rose by about 1%, which is more than the aid itself (Werker et al., 2009, p. 227). Domestic saving fell by close to the value of the aid, so the money substituted for saving rather than adding to it. Prices and growth showed no measurable response (Werker et al., 2009, Tables 2 and 3, pp. 231 and 236).

Then the finding that concerns this module. When the oil price rises, workers from those same countries who are employed in the Gulf also earn more and remit more, in the same years and to the same countries. The oil price moves both flows, not one. The authors tested for it, and once remittances were accounted for, their own estimate of the effect of aid on consumption and on imports fell by up to a third (Werker et al., 2009, p. 240). A study that measures one flow and omits the other attributes to the first what the second paid for.

For this module the last finding is the one that matters. A study that measures one flow and leaves out the other credits the first with what the second paid for. That is why FAR-SIDS looks at aid and remittances in the same household, and why your assignment asks about both flows and not one.

Part two · What the money pays for

29 dollars in every 100 went to obligations before anything else

Fa'alavelaveThe Samoan term for customary obligations such as weddings, funerals, elections and titles. It took 17 dollars of every 100 received, before any ordinary spending.
MisinaleThe annual church donation in Tonga. About a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, and one study had to report household income twice, with and without those transfers.
KavengaThe Tongan term for obligation in general: the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. Meeting them maintains a household's standing and its right to call on others in a crisis.
The approval letter, Ambrym Island, VanuatuA worker who wants to be picked again for seasonal work needs a letter signed by a chief or a pastor, and that person knows what the worker gave to the church and the community while he was at home (Bailey, 2019, p. 11). Giving keeps a household's standing, and it can decide whether the household has an earner abroad next year.
Why this matters

Customary and church obligations take a large and regular share of what a remittance-receiving household spends, and no published indicator records them. A ministry reading its own statistics would count this money as ordinary consumption. Does your government already run a survey that could ask about it, and what would have to be added to that survey?

Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Matautia Smith, F. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Bailey, R. (2019). Observed social impacts on Ambrym Island from seasonal worker programs (2009–2019) [Unpublished report]. Department of Pacific Affairs, Australian National University.

Those were results for whole economies. The next three slides go inside the house, and they start with what the money pays for once it arrives.

Le Dé and colleagues, reading 4, found that in rural Samoa before the 2009 tsunami the largest single use of remittances was neither food nor housing. Households spent about 17 dollars of every 100 received on fa'alavelave, the customary obligations of weddings, funerals, elections and titles, and about 12 dollars on church donations, so 29 dollars of every 100 went to obligations before any ordinary spending, while small business received 3 (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). In Tonga the annual church donation is the misinale, and about a third of remittance transactions are at least partly intended for it, so one study had to report household income twice, once with those transfers and once without them (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007, p. 207). Kavenga is the Tongan term for obligation in general, meaning the duties a household owes to kin, church and community. What is the word on your own island? Most islands have one, and I would like to hear yours.

This spending should not be read as waste, because kavenga and misinale maintain a household's standing and its right to call on others when something goes wrong, and in a country with almost no formal insurance, that standing is what a household relies on in a crisis. However, the spending is invisible in the official figures, because no published wellbeing indicator records it and nobody has yet measured what share of Tongan household income goes to it. A household survey could measure it, and we return to that possibility in part three.

Here is where giving to the church and the community stops being only about standing. Rochelle-lee Bailey has worked with seasonal workers from Ambrym Island in Vanuatu since 2009. A worker who wants to be picked again next season needs an approval letter, and a chief or a pastor signs it. That same person knows what the worker gave to the church, to a wedding and to community projects while he was at home (Bailey, 2019, p. 11). So the obligation has a consequence attached to it: it helps decide who goes next year. Workers manage it. Some set a fixed sum for the church, or for one family, rather than answering every request as it arrives (Bailey, 2019, p. 13). Bailey calls this competing interests in the ownership of a worker's money, and she finds that most workers give back to their communities, because the obligations were settled long before the money was earned (Bailey, 2019, p. 14). That is documented for Ambrym and not for Tonga, so whether the same holds on your island is a question I put back to you.

Part two · What the money becomes over time

Money that has come for forty years is used differently from money that has just started

A coefficientThe number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. Here, for every extra dollar of remittances a Tongan household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher.
What it does not showThe result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference between Tonga and Fiji by the age of the migration corridor.
A question for you

On your island, how long has money been coming from abroad, and does the family you know plan around it, or treat each transfer as a windfall?

Why this matters

Whether a household can invest a transfer depends on how long and how regularly the money has been arriving, and not only on how much. Tongan families have planned around remittances for four decades and put part of them into business; Fijian families, whose flow is younger and less regular, did not. For a ministry, the age and the regularity of a flow are facts about the flow, and a survey that records only the amount misses both.

Sources

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

The last slide was what the money pays for. This one is what it becomes over time. Brown and Leeves, reading 2, asked the same questions in the same year in Tonga and in Fiji to find out what remittances pay for once they arrive. They report the answer as a coefficient, which is the number a statistical model gives for how much one thing changes when another rises by one. In Tonga the coefficient on business income was 0.52, which means that for every extra dollar of remittances a household received, its business income was on average 52 cents higher. In Fiji there was no such effect, and the only consistent result was lower wage income, meaning that people worked fewer paid hours (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 6).

The result is an association measured at one point in time, and the authors state that it does not prove the dollar caused the business. They explain the difference by the age of the migration corridor. Tongans have migrated regularly for four decades, so families can plan around the money and invest part of it, whereas migration from Fiji is more recent and the money arrives less predictably. For a ministry, this means that how long the money has been arriving and how regularly it comes matter as much as the amount.

Hold on to that word, time, because it comes back on the next slide from the other direction. Here, forty years of a regular flow let households plan and invest. On the next slide we ask what the household lost when the earner left, and that loss also changes with time. So before we go on, the question on the screen: on your island, how long has money been coming from abroad, and does the family you know plan around it or treat each transfer as a windfall?

Part two · What the migrant no longer contributes

The household gains the money and loses the worker

The simple method

Income minus remittances

Take the household’s income, subtract the remittances, and call the difference the gain from migration. The method assumes that the person who left would have earned nothing at home.

The counterfactual · Latin America

What the migrant would have earned if they had stayed

Once it is counted, the measured fall in extreme poverty shrinks from 14% to 3% (Acosta et al., 2008).

A migration lottery as evidence · Tonga

Chance decided who left, so the comparison is fair

New Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration. In the first year the migrants’ families had lower total income than the families who lost the ballot, and the remittances did not make up the loss (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007).

A question for you

Think of a family you know with someone abroad. In the first year after they left, was the family better off or worse off? And ten years on?

Why this matters

A transfer counts as a gain for a household only once you know what the household lost when the earner left, and that loss changes with time: the first year is often the hardest, and years later the money itself may thin out as the migrant settles. National figures record neither the loss nor the thinning. That is why the FAR-SIDS survey asks each household who left, when, and what they used to do at home.

Sources

Acosta, P., Calderón, C., Fajnzylber, P., & López, H. (2008). What is the impact of international remittances on poverty and inequality in Latin America? World Development, 36(1), 89–114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2007.02.016

McKenzie, D., Gibson, J., & Stillman, S. (2007). Moving to opportunity, leaving behind what? Evaluating the initial effects of a migration policy on incomes and poverty in source areas. New Zealand Economic Papers, 41(2), 197–223. https://doi.org/10.1080/00779950709558509

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2011). The impacts of international migration on remaining household members: Omnibus results from a migration lottery program. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 93(4), 1297–1318. https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00129

Gibson, J., McKenzie, D., & Stillman, S. (2013). Accounting for selectivity and duration-dependent heterogeneity when estimating the impact of emigration on incomes and poverty in sending areas. Economic Development and Cultural Change, 61(2), 247–280. https://doi.org/10.1086/668276

When a son moves to Auckland and sends money home, the household gains the money and loses the son, meaning his wages, his work on the family plantation and his care for his parents. The simple method takes the household's income, subtracts the remittances, and calls the difference the gain from migration, which assumes that the son would have earned nothing if he had stayed.

Economists call the missing element the counterfactual, meaning what would have happened otherwise. Acosta and colleagues calculated the effect both ways for Latin America: when the migrant's lost earnings are ignored, migration reduces extreme poverty by about 14%, and when they are counted, the reduction is about 3%. For Mexico the direction reverses, so that once lost earnings are counted, migration is measured as increasing poverty (Acosta et al., 2008, Table 9).

The Tongan evidence is unusually strong, because New Zealand ran a ballot for Tongan migration and chance decided who left, so the families who lost the ballot are a fair comparison for the families of those who won. In the first year, the winners' families had lower total income, lower earnings, lower farm and business income and less food grown at home, and the remittances did not make up the loss (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007). A later paper by the same authors on the Samoan ballot found the opposite result in the first years: poverty fell among the families left behind. But both the remittances and the family's own farm income were lower the longer the migrant had been away, so the authors warn that the gain may be short lived (Gibson, McKenzie and Stillman, 2013). That does not mean the families end up poorer than before the migrant left; it means the money thins out as the migrant settles abroad, and the plot at home is not planted as it was. Time therefore works in both directions. On the last slide, decades of a regular flow let Tongan households invest. Here, years away let the money and the farm both decline. Before crediting a remittance to a household, ask what the person who sent it would have earned, grown and cared for if they had stayed.

Part two · Tonga in the national accounts and in the household

Tonga read through the national accounts, and read through one household

Read through the national accounts: more money arrives, and the country is classed as upper middle income
  • Remittances were 39.2% of national output in 2024, among the highest shares in the world.
  • Net aid was 20.3% of gross national income in 2023, and 50.7% in 2022, the year of the eruption.
  • Donor partners funded 46.5% of the national budget for 2023 to 2024, 364.7 of 784.2 million pa'anga.
  • Income per person was 6,270 US dollars in 2024 (World Bank, n.d.), above the 4,636 dollar line for upper middle income, and Tonga has never been on the United Nations list of least developed countries.
Read through one household: the earner is gone, and part of the money is spoken for
  • The person who earns the money is somewhere else. The wages he would have earned at home and the food he would have grown are in none of these figures, and neither is his absence.
  • Part of what arrives is promised before it is spent. In rural Samoa, 29 dollars in every 100 paid customary and church obligations first; nobody has measured the Tongan share.
  • Moving the money costs the household about 8 dollars in every 100 on the New Zealand and Australia corridors, and that is taken off the household, not off the national figure.
  • What the household gained and what it gave up are recorded in different places, and only one of the two is published.
A claim for discussion

A country can receive more money every year and rise into a higher income class, while the household that receives the money is no better off, because the accounts count the money that arrived and not the person who left to earn it.

The FAR-SIDS website: Tonga

This is the slide I most want you to argue with. It sets the same country down twice. I am going to build it around one household, so that the numbers stay attached to people.

Take a family in Ha’apai: a mother, three children, a grandmother, and a father who leaves in April on a seasonal work visa and comes home in November. Most of what is on this slide follows from that one arrangement.

Read it first through the national accounts, which is what a finance ministry and a donor read. The father sends money home. A bank or a transfer company reports it, the central bank adds it to the national total, and it crosses into Tonga’s figures. Multiply that household by the thousands in the same position and you have the left card. Remittances came to 39.2% of national output in 2024, one of the highest shares anywhere. Net aid was 20.3% of national income in 2023. In 2022, the year of the eruption, it was 50.7% of national income, which means that the aid Tonga received that year was equal to half of everything its residents earned. Donor partners paid for 46.5% of the national budget for 2023 to 2024, 364.7 of 784.2 million pa'anga (Parliament of Tonga, 2023). And income per person was 6,270 US dollars in 2024, above the World Bank's line for upper middle income, and Tonga has never been on the United Nations list of least developed countries. Notice what this card does and does not say. It does not say Tonga is well off; a country that depends this much on aid and on relatives abroad is not. It says that more money arrives from outside every year, and that income per person has risen far enough for the country to be classed as upper middle income. Those are the two facts a finance ministry and a donor read, and they are true.

Now read the same family through the household, which is the right card, and I want to take it in three steps.

First, the father is not in the house. For seven months of the year the household has lost his work: the wages he would have earned at home, the plot he would have planted, the fishing, the repairs, the school run. Nothing in the left card records any of that. Those accounts count the money that arrived and not the person who left to earn it, because that is what they were built to measure.

Second, part of what arrives is promised before it is spent. You saw the Samoan figures an hour ago: 29 dollars in every 100 went to customary obligations and church giving before any ordinary spending (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). Nobody has measured the Tongan share. You now know why that gap matters, and you know which instrument could close it.

Third, the money costs something to move. Sending 200 US dollars from New Zealand or Australia to Tonga cost about 8 dollars in every 100 in the third quarter of 2025 (World Bank, 2025a). That comes off the household, and it appears nowhere in the left card.

So here is the claim on the screen, and it is a claim rather than a fact: a country can receive more money every year and rise into a higher income class, while the household that receives the money is no better off, because the accounts count the money that arrived and not the person who left to earn it. I want you to disagree with that sentence, and I will give you the strongest objection myself, which is that I chose the right card in order to make the point. I did. A fair reply would be that the father chose to go, that the family has more money than it would otherwise have had, that the children are in school because of it, and that a measure which ignores what people choose for themselves is not much of a measure either. If you hold that view, say so, and we will take it up tomorrow.

The Tonga page on the FAR-SIDS website carries both flows from 1995 to 2025 on one chart, with the cyclones and the eruption marked along the bottom. I am opening it now, and you can use it tomorrow for your own island.

The next slide takes the government side of the same account, and it changes what the financial line of your map means.

Part two · What income per person decides

Income per person decides whether aid arrives as a grant or a loan

What a loan does to a budgetIn the year to June 2025 Tonga repaid 29.4 million US dollars of debt, 17.7 million of it to a single creditor, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million (Agence France-Presse, 2026). A figure for what arrived does not say what stayed.
What graduation costs, and what it does notMost partners keep working in a country after it leaves the list. What changes is the terms of the finance, and what is lost outright is the trade access reserved for least developed countries, for which the WTO says there is no perfect substitute (Enhanced Integrated Framework, n.d.). Both systems start from income per person, which counts the seasonal worker's wages and none of the sister's transfers.
A question for tomorrow

When the grant window closes, are families abroad expected to fill the gap? A remittance rebuilds a roof by Christmas. It does not rebuild a road, and the loan that rebuilt the road is repaid out of the budget that also pays for the clinic.

This slide comes from the government side of the account rather than the household side. It tests the same claim as the last slide, and you will want it for the first question of your assignment and for the financial line of your map.

The first is that the national accounts count money arriving and not money leaving. In the year to June 2025 Tonga repaid 29.4 million US dollars of debt, 17.7 million of it to a single creditor, against an infrastructure budget of about 10.1 million. Repayments came to nearly three times what the country budgeted for infrastructure. A figure for what arrived does not tell you what stayed.

The second is that the income measure in the national accounts has a consequence attached to it. This needs explaining, because two different systems are at work here and they are easy to confuse.

The first system is the United Nations category of least developed countries. A country enters it, and leaves it, on three criteria: income per person, the Human Assets Index, which covers health and schooling, and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index. The Committee for Development Policy reviews the list every three years. To be recommended for graduation, a country has to meet the thresholds on two of the three criteria at two consecutive reviews. The Economic and Social Council then endorses the recommendation, the General Assembly takes note of it, and the country is given a preparatory period, normally three years and recently five or six, before graduation takes effect (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, n.d.).

Small island states have been leaving that category for twenty years. Cabo Verde graduated in 2007, Maldives in 2011, Samoa in 2014, Vanuatu in 2020 and São Tomé and Príncipe in 2024. Solomon Islands is scheduled for 2027. Kiribati and Tuvalu have been recommended by the Committee, and the Council has deferred them at every review since 2015 on grounds of vulnerability: on UNCTAD's 2018 figures they carried the highest economic vulnerability scores of any small island developing state, 76.5 and 76.3 (UNCTAD, 2021). And for the Comoros the Committee deferred its decision to the 2027 review (United Nations Office of the High Representative, n.d.).

What does a country lose when it graduates? Not aid itself, and it is worth being exact about that. Most development partners keep working in a country after it graduates. What changes is the kind of assistance and the terms of the concessional finance. What is lost outright is the set of measures reserved for least developed countries: duty-free and quota-free access to the European Union under Everything But Arms, and the equivalent schemes run by Canada and Japan, together with the more generous rules of origin attached to them, and special treatment at the World Trade Organization. For a country whose exports are fish or clothing, that is a real margin, and the WTO's position is that there is no perfect substitute for those preferences: what a graduating country ends up with depends on what it can negotiate with each trading partner (Enhanced Integrated Framework, n.d.).

The second system is the one that applies to Tonga, because Tonga has never been a least developed country. The World Bank classifies countries by gross national income per person, and that classification is the main test for access to its grants and its cheapest lending. By that measure Tonga is an upper middle income country, and on that measure alone it would no longer qualify for World Bank grants. It keeps them because the Bank makes an exception for small island economies, and reading 1, the State of SIDS Report summary, sets that exception out.

Now notice what the two systems have in common, and it takes us back to the scale slide. Both of them start from income per person. Gross national income counts what residents earn, and a seasonal worker who is away for seven months is still counted as living at home, so her wages are in it. It does not count what a sister who settled in Auckland ten years ago sends back. So the earnings of people who are absent from the household raise the measure that decides whether a country keeps its concessional finance, and the transfers the household receives do not enter that measure at all. An exception had to be written so that Tonga did not lose its grants. Whether that exception is the right answer, and whether a vulnerability measure should sit beside the income measure rather than behind it, is worth arguing about, and it is a good question for your first assignment.

For your map, this is the teal line on the financial asset: does aid reach your island as a grant or as a loan, and who repays it. And here is a question to hold for tomorrow. When the grant window closes, as it has for Jamaica, are families abroad expected to fill the gap? Look at what each flow can build. A remittance rebuilds a roof by Christmas. It does not rebuild a road, and the loan that rebuilt the road is repaid out of the same budget that pays for the clinic.

Part two ends here, so put it back beside the question of the week: what does each kind of money do for the people in the house? You now have part of the answer. Aid and remittances reach the house by different paths, decided by different people from different places. Part of what arrives is spoken for before it is spent, and what the household gives up, the absent earner, the fee, the repayments, appears in no national figure. Part three gives you a tool for asking the rest of the question in an orderly way, for your own island.

Part three

From the national figure to the household

A national total records how much money arrived. The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework is the tool for asking what a household did with the money, who decided, and what the household lives on. Tomorrow you apply it to your own island.

What the household shows that the national figure cannot

Who received each flow, what it paid for, and who decided: whether more money arriving made a household better off.

The framework

Five assets, who controls each of them, and the conditions the household lives in.

From the map to one recommendation

How a finding on the map becomes an action a ministry can take, and the four tests it passes.

In part two you saw that the same country can look supported in the national accounts and stretched inside the household, and that the difference comes down to who received the money and who decided what it was for. Part three gives you a tool for asking those two questions in an orderly way. A national total records how much money arrived, and the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework is the tool that describes what that money meant for the households that received it. Everything in this part is a tool you will use tomorrow and in your assignment, and I will introduce the framework through one worked example.
