Before the framework, I want to answer a question you may be asking: why go to the household at all, when the national figure is published every year? Start with a question of your own. The last time money came into your house from outside, who decided what it was for, and would anybody in a ministry have a way of knowing? Keep your answer.

Wellbeing happens in a house, not in a national account. A country can receive more and a family can be no better off, and the Tonga slide showed you how that happens. The three cards on the screen are three moments where the national figure and the household give different answers, and where the difference changes what a government can do.

The first is Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa, which made landfall on 28 October 2025. The national figure says that remittances were 3.49 billion US dollars in 2025 and, by December, 13.6% higher than a year before (Bank of Jamaica, 2026), and it is easy to read that as the whole island being covered. The household survey says something else: 42.5% of the poorest fifth of households receive remittances, against 61.0% of the richest fifth (PIOJ and STATIN, 2021, p. xii). Now watch the months. Net remittances fell 8.3% in October, while transfer offices were shut and there was no power, and in December they were 13.6% above the year before (Bank of Jamaica, 2025; Bank of Jamaica, 2026). A household with a relative in Florida had money for a roof by Christmas. A household with nobody abroad, which is more often a poor household, was waiting for the aid chain we drew on the who decides slide. Here is what the state's money did in the same months. Within weeks the development banks and the IMF put together a package worth 6.7 billion US dollars over three years, more than half of it loans (World Bank, 2025). The government created a reconstruction authority, NaRRA, by law on 27 May 2026, and on 8 September 2026 the Prime Minister said that building contracts were only now being signed (Office of the Prime Minister, 2026a; Jamaica Gleaner, 2026b). The state's own home repair grants reached a first 1,234 families in February (Office of the Prime Minister, 2026b). In the same seven months, Jamaicans abroad sent home 1.85 billion US dollars, 7.7% more than a year earlier, and sixty cents of every extra dollar went to Kingston and St Andrew, not to the western parishes that took the worst of the storm (Jamaica Gleaner, 2026a). So the remittances were fast and went where the relatives were. The public money was slow and is meant to go where the damage was. A ministry that reads only the national figure sends recovery money to both kinds of household in the same way. A ministry that knows which households receive remittances can send the public money first to the households that do not.

The second is Tonga and the seasonal work agreement. On 30 June 2026, 3,715 Tongans held PALM visas in Australia (DEWR, 2026). The government that signed that agreement reads the national accounts, where remittances were 39% of GDP in 2024, and the agreement looks like a success. What does it look like from the house? For permanent migration we have the lottery evidence: in the first year the families of the men who left had lower total income, because the money did not replace the plot, the fishing and the wages he would have earned at home (McKenzie, Gibson and Stillman, 2007). For the seasonal scheme nobody has measured the household side in Tonga in the same way. So when Tonga decides whether to ask for more places, a shorter season or a different way of choosing who goes, it decides without the one figure that would say whether families are better off. That is a decision you could help with, and it is the kind of question the FAR-SIDS survey is built to answer.

The third is an aid programme that pays cash to households. In Jamaica that programme is PATH, which pays a household each month when the children attend school and the clinic, and it is funded by a World Bank loan. When PATH starts paying a household, what does the sister abroad do? Across the studies that Nikolov and Bonci (2020) reviewed, private transfers fell when a public benefit arrived, in some settings by as much as 91%. In Nicaragua and Honduras, conditional cash transfers did not reduce remittances at all (Olinto and Nielsen, 2008). So the answer differs by place, and a ministry cannot know which answer applies to its own programme unless a survey records how much arrives from abroad and who decides. If the sister sends less, the household is not better off by the full payment, and the ministry has paid for part of what the family was already getting.

So: who received, what it paid for, who decided, and what the household gave up. Those four things decide whether a household is better off, and the framework on the next slides is the way to ask them in order.

Part three · The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (DFID, 1999)

The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework: five assets a household lives on

Human

Skills, knowledge, the ability to work, and good health

What lets the people in the house pursue a livelihood at all (DFID, 1999).

Social

Networks, group membership, and relationships of trust and reciprocity

The people a household can draw on, and the obligations that keep it in good standing with them; kavenga and misinale sit here.

Physical

Basic infrastructure and producer goods

Shelter, transport, water, energy and communications, and the tools and equipment a household works with: the house, the boat, the road, the water tank.

Financial

Savings, credit, and regular inflows such as pensions and remittances

DFID lists remittances here by name. A transfer arrives as a financial asset and can become any of the other four.

Natural

The natural resource stocks a livelihood draws on

Land, water, reef, soil and forests, and the flows that come from them: a catch, a crop, clean water.

The pentagon as DFID drew it, with the five assets in the order of the guidance sheets. A transfer arrives at the financial point and can travel to any of the other four. Source: Department for International Development (1999), Sustainable livelihoods guidance sheets, section 2.3.

Why this matters

Wellbeing is not one figure. The framework treats what a household lives on as five kinds of asset, and a transfer that arrives as cash can become any of them: a school fee (human), a church contribution (social), a water tank (physical), a saving (financial), a boat that fishes the reef (natural). The national figures record the arrival and stop there. Once you can say which asset a transfer became, and who decided, you can ask which flow supports which part of a household's living, and that is the question behind FAR-SIDS: how foreign aid and remittances shape wellbeing in small island developing states.

Sources

Chambers, R., & Conway, G. (1992). Sustainable rural livelihoods: Practical concepts for the 21st century (IDS Discussion Paper No. 296). Institute of Development Studies. https://www.ids.ac.uk/publications/sustainable-rural-livelihoods-practical-concepts-for-the-21st-century/

Scoones, I. (1998). Sustainable rural livelihoods: A framework for analysis (IDS Working Paper No. 72). Institute of Development Studies. https://www.staff.ncl.ac.uk/david.harvey/AEF806/Sconnes1998.pdf

Department for International Development. (1999). Sustainable livelihoods guidance sheets. https://www.livelihoodscentre.org/documents/114097690/114438878/Sustainable+livelihoods+guidance+sheets.pdf

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

A household does not live on money alone. The framework on the screen is a way of setting out everything it does live on, and it lists five things. The framework calls them capitals. I will call them assets.

Human assets are skills, knowledge, the ability to work and good health. They are what lets the people in the house pursue a livelihood at all.

Social assets are the people a household can call on: kin, neighbours and the church, together with the obligations that keep it in good standing with them. Kavenga and the misinale belong here.

Physical assets are the things the household owns and uses: the house, the boat, the tools, the road it drives on, the water tank.

Financial assets are savings, credit, and regular inflows, and the guidance sheets name remittances among them. The transfer we have counted all afternoon arrives here. What stays here is what the household can keep as cash, put aside, or borrow against, and that depends on whether the money comes regularly and whether it arrives as a deposit or as notes at a counter.

Natural assets are land, reef, soil and water. They are what the island itself provides.

Give me one example of each from your own island before we go on.

Where does this come from? Robert Chambers and Gordon Conway set the idea out in 1992. Ian Scoones built it into a framework in 1998 with four assets. The British aid department added physical, and published all five as the pentagon you have on the screen, drawn here in the same order as the guidance sheets: human at the top, then natural, financial, physical and social (DFID, 1999).

Here is why the pentagon matters for this module. A transfer arrives as one thing, cash, and it can end up as any of the other four. A remittance that pays a school fee has become a human asset. One that pays the misinale has become a social asset. One that buys a water tank has become a physical asset. The figures you found in part one record the arrival and stop there, so they cannot say which of the five the money became. That is the question your map answers tomorrow, and each of these five assets is a row on the map.

That is also where this module meets the research behind it. Wellbeing is not one figure. The framework treats it as five, and once you can say which of the five a transfer reached, you can ask which flow supports which part of a household's living. That is the question FAR-SIDS sets out to answer, how foreign aid and remittances shape wellbeing in small island developing states, and this framework is what gives the question a structure. It says what to measure, and it lets you see aid and remittances reaching different assets rather than adding up to one total.

A revision of this framework was published in 2022, and it is reading 3 on your list. It keeps the assets and puts the power and the context around them. That is the next slide.

Sources

Natarajan, N., Newsham, A., Rigg, J., & Suhardiman, D. (2022). A sustainable livelihoods framework for the 21st century. World Development, 155, Article 105898. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.105898

Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. (2026). PALM scheme data publication, June 2026 [Data set]. Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. https://www.palmscheme.gov.au/

Bank of Jamaica. (2011). Remittances to Jamaica: Findings from a national survey of remittance recipients. https://www.boj.org.jm/uploads/pdf/papers_pamphlets/papers_pamphlets_Remittances_to_Jamaica_-_Findings_from_a_National_Survey_of_Remittance_Recipients.pdf

The pentagon in the middle of that drawing is the one from the last slide. Everything around it is what the 2022 revision adds, and this is reading 3 on your list. The authors' charge against the original is that it is not political enough. In their words, politics was rendered as background noise, everywhere but at the same time nowhere. So they surround the assets with the power and the context that the original left in the background, and three of those parts become the questions under the house on your map.

The first is relational power: class, gender, ethnicity, caste and other material power relations. The authors call it an equally critical and all too easily overlooked element in building, shaping and sustaining livelihoods, and they place it beside the assets to correct what they call methodological individualism, which is the habit of explaining a household by looking only inside it. On your map it becomes the question who decided. Two examples from our own material. Of the 3,715 Tongans on Pacific Australia Labour Mobility visas in June 2026, 3,095 were men, about eight in ten, because the fruit picking corridors recruit men and the care corridors recruit women, so the work on offer decides who leaves the house (DEWR, 2026). At the receiving end, in Jamaica's national survey of 2,072 people receiving remittances, three in four were women (Bank of Jamaica, 2011), and that survey was run in 2010, so the most recent national evidence on who receives in Jamaica is fifteen years old. Receiving is not controlling. The question to ask is who could spend the money without asking anyone.

The second is what the authors call transforming structures and processes, along the bottom: policies and norms, institutions and social groups, formal and informal, working at the local, national and global level at once. For this module, that is where a seasonal labour agreement between two governments sits, where a donor's country strategy sits, and where the rule that decides which households a programme enrols is written. On your map it becomes the question who was left out, because the rule that lets a household in is the rule that keeps another out.

The third is the context on the left. The original called it a vulnerability context, and the revision calls it a livelihood context and landscape, because it holds opportunity as well as risk. On your map it becomes the last shock. Take a cyclone. It destroys the house, which is physical. It damages the land, which is natural. It sends the household to church and kin, which are social. It forces the cash, which is financial, to replace what was lost, and whoever holds that cash decides whether what is left pays a school fee or a church obligation. So one cyclone touches all five assets, and the person holding the cash decides what is left for the school fee.

Two more things are on the drawing, and I want you to be able to read them. The band along the top, the politics of influence and access, is about who can reach the institutions that hold the assets: a family with a cousin in the ministry reaches a programme that a family without one never hears of, and the authors call this band the part of the framework that explains the who, how and why of a livelihood. On your map it sits inside the question who was left out. And on the right, where the original framework had strategies and outcomes, the revision writes livelihoods in flux, because a household does not plan a strategy and arrive at an outcome; it revises what it does every season, after every price change and every storm. That is why the last shock is one of the four questions, and why the answer changes from year to year.

The revision also narrows what sits in the assets shape to financial and physical, and moves human, social and political into relational power, and land, water and climate into the context. This module keeps all five assets around the house, because you need all five to say what a transfer touched, and adds these three questions under it. The next slide shows the whole drawing filled in for one country.

This is the map you draw tomorrow, started for Jamaica so that you can see what goes on a line and where it comes from, and only started, because the full one is for after you have drawn your own. One house in the middle, the five assets around it, two colours: teal for what a donor paid for, coral for what a relative paid for.

Read the human line with me. In teal, PATH, the cash transfer paid on school attendance and clinic visits, funded by a World Bank loan; that came from the World Bank project pages we opened this afternoon. In coral, school fees and medical bills, and a number: of every dollar received by households that receive every month, 14 cents went to education and 7 to medical bills. That came from the Bank of Jamaica’s 2010 survey of 2,072 people receiving remittances (Bank of Jamaica, 2011), the one survey in Jamaica that asked what the money was used for.

Now the physical line. In teal, roads, water and school rebuilding, financed by the Inter-American Development Bank, the World Bank, the Caribbean Development Bank and China; the lenders’ project pages again. In coral, housing and repairs, 10 cents in every dollar, from the same 2010 survey. Two lines, and already the two colours point at different things: a relative pays for a school term, a lender pays for a road.

One question under the house is filled in, who decided. On the aid side, the lender and the ministry, years ahead, and then a means test that a poor household can fail. On the remittance side, the honest answer is that the 2010 survey never asked; what it did record is that three in four recipients were women (Bank of Jamaica, 2011). That is what a line looks like when the source runs out: you say what was asked, what was not, and where you looked.

The other three assets and the other three questions stay empty today. Before tomorrow, think about what you would write on them for your own island, and where you would look. Tomorrow you draw the whole thing, and then I show you Jamaica finished, so you can compare.

Part three · The indicators ministries publish

Six figures a ministry already publishes, and where each one gets its numbers

Suppose Jamaica sends recovery money to the households that do not receive remittances. A year later, which of these six would show whether those households are better off, and what would have to be added to make it show that?

The indicatorWhat it countsWhere its numbers come from
GDP per person
The value of what the country produced in a year, divided by its peopleThe national accounts
Poverty headcount, and the poverty gap
How many people live below a poverty line, and how far below itThe household survey
Human Development Index
Income, schooling and life expectancy, in one national figureNational statistics, not a household survey
Multidimensional Poverty Index
Ten deprivations in health, education and living standards, house by houseThe household survey
Food Insecurity Experience Scale
Eight questions on running short of food, and how badlyThe household survey
Gini coefficient
How unequal income is across households, in one numberThe household survey
An indicatorA single measure, published on the same definition for many countries, usually once a year. These six are the ones small island governments most often report.
Question three of the assignmentWhich indicators would show whether your recommendation is working: which of these six could do it, what would have to be added, and what would still be missing.
Why this matters

Four of the six come from the household survey: the poverty headcount and gap, the Multidimensional Poverty Index, the food insecurity scale and the Gini. Those four can carry the answer once that survey records which households receive a transfer, how regularly, and who decides. None of the six records that today. Question three asks which of them could show your recommendation working, what would have to be added, and what would still be missing.

Take the first card from the last slide but one. Jamaica sends recovery money to the households that do not receive remittances. A year later, how would the ministry know whether those households are better off? It publishes six figures, and the table shows what each one counts and where its numbers come from, because the answer to that question, and question three of your assignment, depends on that last column. Do not decide yet that none of them can help. Several can.

GDP per person is the value of what is produced inside the country in a year, divided by the population, and it comes from the national accounts. It is good at comparing the size of economies and following growth over years. A transfer from abroad is not production inside the country, so it enters this figure only through what the household then buys from a producer at home.

The poverty headcount is the share of the population below a poverty line, and it is good at counting how many people are poor and whether that count is falling. Its companion, the poverty gap index, records how far below the line a household sits, so a transfer that lifts a poor household without lifting it across the line shows up in the gap. Both come from the household survey, which is worth remembering for question four.

The Human Development Index combines income, schooling and life expectancy into one figure a year. It was published from 1990 to show that a country can grow richer without becoming healthier or better schooled, and it is good at comparing countries on all three at once. It is a national average built from national statistics, and the inequality adjusted version published beside it shows how evenly the three are shared.

The Multidimensional Poverty Index counts ten deprivations across health, education and living standards, household by household, from survey data rather than from the national accounts. It is good at showing which deprivations overlap in the same house, and of the six it comes closest to the five assets we have been working with.

The Food Insecurity Experience Scale is eight questions put to the household, placing it on a range from being worried about food to going without. It is good at recording how severe a shortage was, not only whether it happened. In Kingston, Thomas-Hope used a scale of this kind, the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale, and found that households receiving remittances were no less likely to run short of food, while among poor households the shortage was less severe (Thomas-Hope, 2025). A measure that recorded only whether a shortage happened would not have found that.

The Gini coefficient summarises how unequal income is across households in one number, from the same household survey, and it is good at showing whether growth, or a transfer, widened or narrowed the gap between rich and poor households.

Now the part I would like you to argue with me about. Which of these six could show whether the households that do not receive remittances are better off a year on? Tell me before I do. GDP per person and the Human Development Index would not move for those households alone, because they are national figures. The headcount and the poverty gap could, because they come from the same household survey a remittance section would join, once that survey records which households receive. The multidimensional index could, for the same reason, and it already works house by house. The food insecurity scale could, because it records severity, which is where the Kingston effect showed. So question three is not an argument that the indicators are wrong. It asks which of them can carry the answer, what would have to be added, and what nothing yet records: who in the house receives, how regularly, who decides, and what leaves the house again. That is why question three sits before question four: you name what would show the result before you propose the action.

Before you write it, tell me what you would want to know about your own island that none of these six reports. I will offer a few and you can reject them. Whether an income is regular or occasional, because a regular one can support a loan. What a household owes, and to whom. How many months of the year an adult member is away. What it costs to reach a clinic or a market, which on a country of many islands differs from island to island. How much of the food eaten was grown rather than bought. Some of those could be answered by adding a question to a survey your statistics office already runs. Others could not be measured at all. Saying which is which is part of the work in question three.

One last point. An indicator is chosen as well as measured. A ministry that begins to record what households owe will learn things it may not want to publish, and a measure that nobody in the ministry wants is unlikely to be funded. So when you name the indicators, name also who would use the answer.

Part three · A recommendation a ministry can act on

From the map to one recommendation

  1. A finding on the map. Jamaica: the poorest fifth of households receive remittances least, 42.5% against 61.0% for the richest fifth (PIOJ and STATIN, 2021, p. xii), and the figures behind that are old: households receiving from 2019, who inside the house receives from 2010.
  2. What the ministry cannot see. After Melissa, which households already have a private safety net and which have none.
  3. What would show it. Household receipt by spending group; how regularly the money comes; who in the house receives; and time to recovery, compared between households that receive and households that do not.
  4. One action. About fifteen questions added to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs: cash, goods and bills paid counted separately, who receives, how regularly, and what leaves the house again.
  5. The four tests. An instrument that exists. A cost the budget can bear. A question the government is already asking. A plain statement of what it will not do: it changes how the flow is measured, not how much money arrives.
Question four of the assignment

One recommendation, argued against the four tests

Make one recommendation for your own island, take it through these five steps, and end with the sentence that says what it will not do, in your own words.

Sources

Planning Institute of Jamaica and Statistical Institute of Jamaica. (2021). Jamaica survey of living conditions 2019: Overview. Retrieved September 20, 2026, from https://www.pioj.gov.jm/product/jamaica-survey-of-living-conditions-jslc-2019-overview/

Question four of your assignment asks for one recommendation a ministry could act on. Here is how the Jamaica map leads to a recommendation, in five steps, and the same five steps work for your island.

Step one is a finding on the map. In Jamaica the poorest fifth of households receive remittances least, 42.5% against 61.0% for the richest fifth (PIOJ and STATIN, 2021, p. xii), and the two national figures behind that are old: households receiving is from 2019, and who inside the house receives is from 2010.

Step two is what the ministry cannot see. After Hurricane Melissa the government had to decide who gets public recovery money, and it could not tell a household with a reliable relative in Florida from a household with nobody.

Step three is what would show it. GDP per person would not move for those households alone, for the reason on the last slide. The poverty gap and the household survey behind it could carry part of the answer, and the rest has to be added. Household receipt by spending group. How regularly the money comes, because a regular flow can back a loan and an occasional one buys groceries. Who in the house receives. And how long it takes a household to restore its roof, its income and its children's schooling, compared between households that receive and households that do not.

Step four is one action that produces those measures: about fifteen questions added to the Survey of Living Conditions, which the statistics office already runs. Each question is there because a study somewhere showed what happens without it. Cash, goods and bills paid are counted separately, because Tonga showed what one cash question misses: the national survey of 2001 asked about cash and found 75 households in every hundred receiving, and Brown and Leeves asked about goods, school fees and bills as well in 2004 and found 90 (Brown and Leeves, 2011). A survey that asks only about cash undercounts the barrel and the school fee paid from Florida. Who in the house receives, because the Jamaican survey counts households and not people, and the last time anybody asked who the person was, in 2010, three in four were women (Bank of Jamaica, 2011); a ministry designing a grant to reach women needs the person, not the house. How regularly the money comes, because Brown and Leeves found that Tongan households, with forty years of a regular flow, put part of it into business, 52 cents of business income for every extra dollar, while Fijian households with a younger and less regular flow did not (Brown and Leeves, 2011, Table 6); a regular income can back a loan, and an occasional one buys groceries. And what leaves the house again as church and community giving, because in rural Samoa 29 dollars in every hundred received went to customary obligations and the church before any ordinary spending (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664), and a survey that does not ask counts that money as consumption and overstates what the household kept.

Step five is the four tests on the right of the screen, and the recommendation passes each one. There is an instrument, because the survey is already in the field. The cost is one the budget can bear, because fifteen questions on a form that is already printed and funded need no new survey and no new field round. Somebody is already asking the question, because recovery targeting needs the answer now. And it says plainly what it will not do: it changes how the flow is measured, not how much money arrives, and it will not make aid arrive faster.

Write that last sentence for your own recommendation, in your own words, at the end of your assignment.

Thank you for today. Two kinds of money arrive on an island, and you can now find how much of each arrived, say what the figures leave out, and ask what each one did for the people in the house: what it paid for, who decided, who it reached and who it missed, and what the household gave up.

Tomorrow is yours. First you find the three figures for your own island; if a figure is not published anywhere, write down what you searched for and where you looked, because that absence is a finding and it earns marks. Then you draw the map: one house, the five assets around it, and two colours, a few words on each line. Then you answer the four questions under the house. Then each group presents its map, four minutes, and the classwork and the assignment are written from what is on it. Bring a laptop, and the two things the module outline asks for.

The four steps on the right are the method for any island, whichever island it is. The World Bank pages carry every country and the OECD table carries every aid recipient, so start there. The central bank and the statistics office take digging: search your country’s name with the words central bank or statistics office, open the office’s own site rather than a news article, and look for a menu called Statistics, Economic Reviews or Publications. Old is fine, a PDF is fine, French is fine.

One question to take home, and I would like you to ask it of somebody in your family tonight. If every relative abroad stopped sending money to your island for one year, what would go unpaid first: the school fees, the church contribution, or the roof repair? And who on your island would notice last? Think about which of the five assets each of those is, and who has no relative abroad to lose. Bring your answer tomorrow; it is the first line of your map.

The map: one house, five assets, two colours, four questions

Every group has this page printed, and it is on the VLE as well. It is one drawing. Your island's household is the house in the middle, the five assets it lives on are around it, and two kinds of money arrive: aid from a donor government, in teal, and remittances from a relative abroad, in coral.

The band at the bottom holds your three figures, because everything above it is read against them. Each one carries its unit, its year and its source.

Then the five assets. On each one there are two lines. On the teal line you write what aid paid for on your island under that asset: the programme by name, a road, a school, a water tank, a cash transfer. On the coral line you write what remittances paid for: school fees, a roof, a funeral, a fridge. A few words, not an amount. Where the line comes from a website, write the address beside it. Most of your coral lines will come from a family you know, and you say so. Where you can find nothing, write not found and where you looked, because that is evidence and a guess is not.

Under the house, four questions, each answered for both colours. Who decided what the money was for. Who was left out. What it cost the household that no figure records. And the last shock on your island, named and dated: what arrived, how fast, and who it reached. The map is those three parts and nothing more, and the next slide shows it filled in for Jamaica.

This is the same drawing filled in for Jamaica, which you saw yesterday, and the printed copy is on the VLE beside the blank one. Today I want you to look at it as a piece of work you are about to do, so notice three things: how short each line is, where each line came from, and what the four questions say when you read them across.

First, the length. Every line is a few words: a programme by name, a use, a source in brackets. The amounts sit in the band at the top and nowhere else. If you are writing a sentence on an asset line, you are writing too much.

Second, where the lines came from. The teal lines came from the lenders' pages you opened yesterday, and each one could carry an address. Three of the coral lines came from the Bank of Jamaica's 2010 survey of people receiving remittances, which asked what the money was used for (Bank of Jamaica, 2011). Two coral lines say ask the family, because no survey in Jamaica asks about church and funeral giving, the Christmas barrel, or a fishing boat. On your island, those are the lines you fill from a family you know, and you say that you did. A line that says not found, with where you looked, is a finding. A line filled with a guess is not.

Third, read the four questions across. Who decided: a lender and a ministry years ahead on one side, and on the other a question the 2010 survey never asked. Who was left out: the households that fail the PATH score, and the households with nobody abroad, which are more often the poorest. What it cost the household: the loan repaid from the budget that pays the clinic, and the sender's years away with the fee on every transfer. And the last shock: 6.7 billion US dollars over three years, more than half of it loans, with the first repair grants in February 2026 (World Bank, 2025; Office of the Prime Minister, 2026b), against remittances 13.6% up by December, most of it to Kingston, where the relatives are (Bank of Jamaica, 2026; Jamaica Gleaner, 2026a). Read across, the last question says in one line what no national figure can: the remittances were fast and went where the relatives were, and the public money was slow and is meant to go where the damage was.

This afternoon you build this page for your own island. The lines you cannot fill are the first thing to write about in your assignment.

Where the full wording is

The module document on the VLE carries the full wording of both pieces and the marking criteria.

Both pieces of assessment come out of the map you have just drawn, so you are leaving this room with the material for each of them.

The classwork is 400 to 500 words. Choose the two assets on your map where the two colours differ most. For each one, say what aid paid for and what remittances paid for, who decided each, and why the two flows reach that asset differently on your island. Give every figure its year, what it measures and its source, and attach a photograph of your map, saying which lines came from a source and which from a family you know. Each of you writes your own classwork, and two students in the same group choose different assets.

The assignment is about 2,500 words: a policy diagnostic on one island, your own where possible, written to its ministry of finance or planning, in four parts. One: how aid and remittances arrive, in what amounts and by which routes, and what the figures leave out; start from your three figures. Two: who each flow reaches and who decides, including how gender shapes who migrates, who receives and who decides, and what the last shock showed about who each flow reached and how fast; use the five assets and the four questions as your structure. Three: which indicators would show whether your recommendation is working, which of the ones the ministry already publishes could show it and how, what would have to be added, and what would still be missing. Four: one recommendation the government can act on, tested against the four tests from yesterday, and a plain sentence at the end saying what it will not do.

Every figure carries a named source: your country's statistical releases and central bank publications as well as peer reviewed studies. The module document on the VLE carries the full wording. Both pieces are marked on three things: your use of the framework, your use of evidence with the year and the source beside each figure, and whether your recommendation is feasible.

ISS5200 · 20 and 21 October 2026

Thank you

If your island became a place nobody had to leave, what would replace the money that relatives send home, and who would decide what it was for?

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Maltaroxane.dewaegh@um.edu.mt

Thank you, all of you. Two days ago the two flows were two national figures. Now you have drawn where each one reaches a household on your own island, who decided, who was left out and what it cost, and you have seen where the published figures stop and where your own knowledge begins. That is the material for your classwork and your assignment, and it is also the method: the three figures, the drawing, and the questions you asked at home.

One question to keep, and I do not have the answer to it. Every remittance on your map is a decision by somebody who left. The sister in Auckland, the father on a seasonal visa, the cousin in Florida: each of them is sending money because there was more to earn somewhere else. So imagine your island became a place nobody had to leave. The coral lines on your map would thin out and, in time, disappear. What would replace the money? A wage on the island, a government programme, a loan, nothing? And who would decide what it was for: the person who earned it, a ministry, or a lender? If you can answer that for your island, you have written the last page of your assignment before you have started it. I would like to read it.
